en: *Record of Verified Accounts of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll One (with Preface), compiled by Meng Xianzhong,
Assistant Administrator of Zizhou. Now, as for *Prajñā*,
it is the mother of wisdom of all Buddhas, the subtle essence of the Ultimate Way, and the spring of the ocean of Dharma.
The source is truly the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. It cuts off the path of language; it extinguishes the sphere of mental activity.

It transcends names, marks, realms, and sense-bases; it is beyond all designations and fails to reach them through investigation. It is detached from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it lies ever further beyond the explanations of intellect and consciousness.
There is no practice and no attainment; thus one brings their merit to fulfillment. There is no abiding and no defilement; thus one perfects their wisdom.

For those who explore its subtlety, every action is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); for those who penetrate its principle, every movement is a Buddha-activity. This extends even to the twelve classes of scripture.
The eighty-four thousand dharmas rival the brilliance of the three celestial bodies; looking up at the radiance of wisdom, they share its same luster.
Like the five thoroughfares vying for traffic, they enter the True Vehicle upon a common track. Only in stillness and solitude does it respond when moved;
without deliberation or thought, sincerity ensures a certain response. Should one possess even a single moment of pure faith and uphold these four verses, their merit shall be immeasurable.
Boundless and vast, it is equal to the Dharma-realm; its fruition is neither born nor extinguished, ultimately identical to empty space.
Thus, it can cause the armies of the asuras to flee afar upon hearing its sound, and the cavalry of Pāpīyas to retreat in haste following its resonance.
The hooks, claws, saw-like fangs, and sharp points are blunted and their keenness crushed; the surging tides and raging fires subside their waves and withdraw their flames.
When the miasmic vapors of the *li* (pronounced *lei*) coalesce like smoke, poison cannot harm; when the opposing ranks join like gathering clouds, blades cannot wound.

This encompasses all conscious beings and extends by analogy to all categories. It is just as a great bell, being empty, receives sound: its resonance does not fail to rise when struck. Or as a bright mirror, suspended on high:
whatever object comes before it is thereby revealed. Thus we know that the realms of the hidden and the manifest harmonize in praise, and this is why the myriad species offer such profound sincerity.
Śakra and Brahmā protect and sustain it; a hundred deities attend and guard it by its power.

Now, taking its spiritual efficacy as the basis—its extraordinary traces being particularly manifest, clearly revealing what is transmitted in the scriptures and encountered by the ears and eyes—it has been compiled into three fascicles, divided into six chapters.
There are those who, upon seeing the virtuous, aspire to equal them; and upon hearing of righteousness, act with courage.

They are like the son who polishes jade or the guest who guards the sword—like Zhou Chu meeting Zhi Shiheng, who cleared away the three横行 (horizontal evils); or like Zhong You encountering Confucius, who was ranked among the Four Categories.
Is benevolence far off? If one desires it, it can be reached. Although we may not suffice to fully develop the Sage’s teachings or brilliantly propagate the Great [Dharma],...
I have composed this so that it may be passed down to my descendants and serve as an encouragement for those of like mind.
It was completed on the eighth day of the fourth month, the Ren-shen day, in the year of Wu-wu (the 6th year of the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang).
Chapter One: Saving and Protecting (with preface, nineteen sections). Chapter Two: Extending Life (with preface, twelve sections).
Chapter One: Saving and Protecting (with preface, nineteen sections).
Formerly, when Master Luan of Lu spoke with a laugh, the Qin army withdrew of its own accord; when Gan Mu rested in repose, the Lord of Wei attained peace.
Upon hearing the name of Zheng Xuan, the host of wicked spirits did not enter, for they feared the transformative influence of the Duke of Tai. Even the divine maidens were moved to grief;

how much more so for the one who precedes the Lord of Images and is the Mother of the Dharma King! Through the Three Insights and Eightfold Path, all is accomplished through contemplation; yet the nine afflictions and six fetters remain.

By means of this, [all afflictions] are extinguished. When there is no name and no form, then all myriad virtues are perfected; when there is no grasping and no practice, then all manifold merits are complete.
Whether upholding or reciting it, it protects the nation and protects the individual: cast into a raging fire, one does not burn;
submerged in surging waves, how could one sink? How great indeed is the power of Prajñā! Therefore, the chapter on "Protection and Rescue" is placed at the beginning of this work.

The *Record of Miraculous Manifestations of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by Xiao Yu states: Liu Jian, the Magistrate of Xingzhou, served as an official supervisor at Fufeng Qiyang during the end of the Sui dynasty.
Initially, he had served under Li Mi; subsequently, he was unjustly implicated and imprisoned in the Grand Court of Justice (*Dali*).
While constantly reciting the *Diamond Prajñāpāramitā*, he had not yet finished two pages when he suddenly fell asleep. In a dream, he saw a...
The Brahman monk said to Jian, "If you can recite the sutras one full time before dawn, you will surely be released.

Jian was immediately startled awake and recited diligently day and night, not daring to slacken even for a moment. After two more days had passed, at noon, an imperial edict of amnesty was suddenly issued.
He was summoned to the court and subsequently granted his release. Later, while Jian was staying at home one night...
Outside his room, he was reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the third watch of the night, he suddenly smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
He rose and followed the scent, but there was no place where it had been burned. By this evidence, he realized it was the power of the merit from reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

From then on, he redoubled his reverence and practiced with diligence day and night, never daring to be indolent; he focused his mind on recitation and retention until he had mastered more than five thousand passages. Upon reaching...
It is not omitted here.
In the *Lángyú Míngbào Shíyí* (Supplementary Records of Miraculous Retribution from the Langyu Region), it is said:

Du Zhiliang of Jingshao served as a military aide (*cánjùnshì*) in the Han Prince Liang’s administration during the Yuánmíng and Suírén periods. After Liang raised troops in rebellion at Bingzhou and was subsequently defeated, Zhiliang—
Together with his subordinates, he was cast into prison. Filled with dread, he worried for his mother, weeping bitterly day and night.

Suddenly, in a dream, he saw a śramaṇa who said, "If you can simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you may escape this calamity. At dawn, he sought out this sūtra and began to recite it.
Aside from the time spent sleeping and eating, he never ceased for even a moment. Before long, the prison officials led the prisoners [to their destination].

During the Fu dynasty, Zhi Liang personally participated in this [punishment]. As the names were called out, everyone was to die; yet when the calling was finished, Zhi Liang invariably leaked the name of someone who had not been listed.
This occurred three times, such that both the master and his subordinates were subjected to flogging. Shortly thereafter, they were pardoned by amnesty.
He died in Huangzhou during the Mingqing era (the character for "qing" is pronounced "she"). (Yu Ling was a relative of Zhi Liang and was previously entrusted with this account.)
During the Linde Yuan year, Dou De-xuan, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan, was dispatched on an inspection tour of Yangzhou.
As he crossed the Huai River, his boat had already moved several dozen paces from the bank. He saw a man on the shore carrying a small bundle;
his appearance was haggard and distressed. As the sun was already setting and there were no other boats in sight, De-xuan took pity on him and ordered [his attendants to assist him].
The boat drew alongside the shore, and he called the man aboard to cross together with him. When they reached midstream, while Xu was eating, he gave the man food as well.
Upon reaching the other side, the man followed behind the horse for several li. Xu asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a King of Ghosts, sent to Yangzhou to pursue Grand Administrator Dou. Xu said, "Grand Administrator Dou..."
"What is your name? he asked. The reply was, "My name is De-xuan. Xuan was the ghost who had been guarding the food. [The Master asked,] "By what means can I avoid this?

It would be most embarrassing for you to leave because of the food I have offered you; please depart first. [The ghost replied,] "You need only recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one thousand times."
He immediately came to inform him. When Xuán arrived in Yangzhou, more than a month had passed; he had completed the required number of recitations for the sutras.

The ghost then appeared and said, "Sir, you have already fulfilled the number of recitations—excellent! You must ultimately accompany me to see the King. Thereupon, the official returned to his room and suddenly fell into a swoon.
After one night had passed, he finally regained consciousness. At first, as he was accompanying the ghost, they arrived at a certain place that was high...
Spears were lined up at the gate like those at the gates of a great province. The ghost said, "Please wait here for a moment;
I shall first report this to the King. The ghost then entered ahead. Xuan hid behind a screen and listened from afar as the King spoke to the ghost, saying, "You devised a scheme for him.
He then had the ghost flogged thirty times. The ghost immediately came out, baring his chest to show [the marks] and saying, "I have taken the staff for you," and then led the way.

Xuán entered [the house] and saw a man dressed in purple descending the steps. They bowed to one another, and the man said, "You possess great merit, yet it is not yet appropriate for you to come here.
I request that you return at once. As Xuán was leaving the gate, he fell into a pit; he then felt as though the ghost had returned to see him.

Seeing Xuán seeking food and paper money, Xuán immediately gave him the food and the paper money. The ghost said, "You still have secondary calamities; you must dispatch a Daoist priest [to perform rites]."
The previous petition had been completed and its karmic retribution (the ghost) had already been extinguished. Once the petitioning was finished, the attendant returned to report to the official.
Xu then requested a Daoist priest to submit another petition. The ghost immediately appeared and said, "The petition did not reach [heaven] because there was a misspelled character.

Xu submitted the petition again, but the ghost said once more, "There is still one character wrong. Xu then personally examined it himself; indeed, they were all misspelled characters. He then ordered [a correction].

In the previous chapter, the spirit said: "This time it has been resolved; there will be no further calamities. De-hyeon questioned the spirit regarding matters of official rank and the year of birth.

The spirit replied: "Your Honor shall serve as Minister of the Ancestral Registry (Chongjeonggyeong), followed by the position of Director of the Palace Administration (Dweungjongam), and subsequently the position of Chief Justice (Daosiseon)."
Next he served as Crown Prince Tuan-yin; next as Minister of the Supreme Bureau of Rites (Siyuan Taichangbo); and next as Left Chancellor. At the age of sixty-four, the ghost vanished.
The offices he subsequently held were exactly as the ghost had foretold. At that time, Daoist practitioners compiled a record of these events, titled *The Record of Master Dou’s Petition to Heaven*.
Xuan also reported this matter to the throne, and by imperial decree it was announced to the ministers, each of whom...
He was instructed to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. (This was recorded by De-xuan’s great-grandson Ti, who passed through Zizhou and recounted the full account.
You Xun of Guangping served as the Assistant Commandant for the Household Affairs of the Gui Prefecture during the Zhengguan period.

He had a daughter who had suffered from a wasting disease for several years. When Xun returned to Hongzhou after his term of office had expired, his daughter’s illness grew increasingly severe. Xun...
He consulted with his wife, Lady Song, saying, "Since this is a malignant illness, I fear it will spread to others later on. If she cannot be saved, we must cast her into the water;
as the俗 (vulgar) saying goes, 'it benefits those who remain. He then had the girl carried out. The girl said, 'I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since my birth.
I request that you read it once more in the master’s Buddha hall before I close my eyes in no small peace. Xu Fu [complied].
When the wife heard these words, she wept profusely at once. She immediately searched for this scripture within the Buddha hall.
As the girl gradually grew weaker, she was unable to see for herself nor speak with her mouth. Xu and his wife, along with the host and others, read it several times for her.
In a brief moment, the girl was then able to open her eyes and point to the scripture, as if seeking to have it read. When they reached...
She was given the scriptures to read, yet she was unable to speak. She observed the scriptures with her eyes and recited them with her mind.
In a short while, a brilliant light shone from within the Buddha hall out into the world, and light also issued forth from inside the scripture case. Everyone was struck with wonder and amazement.
Suddenly, the girl’s head and face broke into a sweat, and in a moment, perspiration covered her entire body; she then fell asleep. After one night had passed, all her ailments were completely cured.

Within no more than ten days, he recovered completely as before. Thereafter, the entire family recited this sutra (as personally related by Changsun Kai, the former Assistant Magistrate of Anjia County in Dingzhou).
Formerly, Wang Chongyi, the Magistrate of Pingqiang County in Jiazhou (Pingqiang pronounced with the *kǔ* and *liáng* finals), was a constant reciter of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

During the Yongchang era, due to his kinship ties, he was repeatedly subjected to legal proceedings and sentenced to the ultimate punishment. As he was about to be executed, he was detained at the Grand Court of Justice (*Dàlǐsì*) in the capital.
While there, Chongyi continued to recite the sūtra without ceasing. Furthermore, he was attended by a maidservant named Zhenru, who [was] highly... in the capital.

[The character for] "xià" (下) is pronounced as "gào". By imperial decree, the Censor Zheng Siqi was dispatched to the capital to fetch Chongyi, ordering him to escort the man himself to the capital for interrogation.
While traveling approximately ten li east of Shan Prefecture, they suddenly encountered a monk standing in the middle of the road.
He said to Chongyi, "Please dismount from your horse for a moment and pay homage to the four directions. The Censor refused; the monk spoke again, saying, "Why are you so stingy?"
He dismounted his horse and prostrated toward the four directions. Once the Censor had dismounted and completed his ritual obeisances to the four quarters, the monk vanished.

The Censor was struck with awe, marveling at this supernatural occurrence. Continuing on his journey, he reached the borders of Luozhou and lay down for the night in the guest hall of the post station.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of human voices saying, "Report to Wang Chongyi: what Zhēnrú has told you is true; this is the 'Prolongation of Life' [incantation]."
"Greatly auspicious. The Censor also heard this. Fearing that the matter would become a source of demonic portents, he reached Luozhou and reported the incident in full to the Emperor.
The Sovereign was greatly alarmed and immediately summoned Chongyi to interrogate him personally: "While you were on the road..."
When asked what caused these strange and ominous events, Chongyi replied, "I truly do not know. He then returned the legal case to the authorities, ordering them to investigate thoroughly.
Before ten days had passed, a general amnesty was proclaimed, and he was granted a pardon from death.
At the age of eighty-seven, he died as the Magistrate of Pingqiang County (as recorded previously by Changsun Kai, the Assistant Magistrate of Anjia County in Dingzhou).
Formerly, Ren Huan, who served as the Judicial Secretary (Sihù) of Dingzhou, was a regular reciter of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
On one occasion, he was sent to Luoyang and was returning with a load of silk and brocade. While traveling by night along the road, he suddenly encountered a band of robbers who came to plunder him;

they killed one of his servants and then pursued Huan with swords and clubs. As the situation became desperate, Huan hid himself behind a tree to take cover. The bandits caught up with him and hacked wildly at him.
Ren Huan tried to put on the ring, but it would not fit; it simply struck against the tree.

The bandits dragged him to another spot, and finding this strange and resentful, they struck him with several more blows from their axes and beat him countless times with clubs, yet he sustained no injury whatsoever.

He then feigned death, and the bandits, believing him truly dead, dispersed together. Ren Huan immediately rose and walked slowly to track down the bandits; the bandits did not travel more than three or four [li].
They were within a *li* [of their destination] and thus could not proceed. Ren Huan remained hidden among the grass.
He heard the bandits conversing with one another, saying, "There has never been water here before; now suddenly there is water flowing from all four sides. This is surely a celestial calamity for us.
One of the bandits said, "When we killed the money-lord earlier, we heard voices in the air saying, 'Do not kill the money-lord! This...

A man was constantly reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. He was a truly virtuous person. A band of thieves were suddenly startled all at once and said to one another, "We have all heard these words.
They all raised their hands and snapped their fingers, sighing and lamenting for a long time. In a short while, the sky gradually grew light, yet the thieves were unable to depart.
Soon thereafter, they were rounded up and captured by the local authorities. Ren Huan subsequently recovered his original belongings.
(As before. Recorded by Changsun Kai, Chief Clerk of Anjia County in Dingzhou.

Wang Changyan was a native of Wannian County in Jingzhao. In the first year of the Jiushi era, while he was managing a pawnshop in Chongren Ward for his cousin Yang Xiyan, he subsequently contracted an abscess that encircled his neck and spread until it reached his ears.
His chest was in pain and he groaned, unable to attend to himself. He then resolved his mind to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From that time on, he never ceased reciting for even a moment. The agony of his sores could no longer be described.
During the night while lying down, he suddenly saw a monk who pressed upon him with a monk’s staff, saying: "Because you have upheld this sūtra, I shall treat your ailment for you."
Thereupon, he was suddenly startled and involuntarily let out a loud cry. Several people inside the hall immediately rose to look at the ulcer that had afflicted him;
there was a flow of fluid from it, amounting to more than one *sheng* of small-bean soup. Because of this single instance, the pain of the carbuncle (*nāḍī*) was instantly relieved.
Thereafter, he devoted himself single-mindedly to upholding [the scripture], reciting it constantly without ceasing. He died at the age of sixty-nine in the first year of the Chang’an era.
[This account of his life until his death was related by his elder cousin, Yang Xiyan.
Wang Lingwang, the Magistrate of Qiao County in Bozhou, used to say of himself that at the age of eight he was able to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He constantly upheld it without fail. Initially, when he had reached the age of twenty (weakuan), he traveled to Lincui in Qiong Prefecture, Jiannan.
In Ku-xian, while traveling along a steep and perilous mountain pass, he suddenly encountered a fierce beast. Wang was struck with terror and found himself at a complete loss for what to do;
he immediately recited the Prajñā Sūtra. The tiger then stopped its advance and began leaping and pawing back and forth. After he had recited it two or three times, [the tiger departed].

He then dragged his tail and fled, drooling several liters of saliva. Furthermore, Ren An, a subordinate official of Anzhou, was transporting grain-tax to Yangzijin when a violent storm suddenly arose.
At that time, there were over five hundred tax-ships on the river, tossing back and forth across the waters.
By dawn, most of the ships had been submerged; however, only Lingwang’s recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* did not cease, as if by divine assistance.
It was solely due to this that he remained unharmed (as related by Wang Qian, Director of the Office of Merit).
Cui Wenjian, the Governor of Fangzhou, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the great incursion of the Tubo, he was captured and taken away.
The Tubo bound him with shackles and guarded him most strictly; yet, with a focused mind, he continued to recite and uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Three days passed, and the lock suddenly opened of its own accord without cause; even when pressed down, it would open again.

The Tibetan general, suspecting that the man had opened the lock by his own private authority, wished to flog him. The man replied, "The lock truly opened by itself; it was not pulled open by my fingers.
The thief asked, "What magical art do you possess such that the lock opens itself? He answered, "It is because I uphold the Vajra."
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. It should be recited for this purpose. The Tibetan said: "I shall now put you in chains.
If you recite the sūtra and the chains open, I will release you and let you return to your country. If you recite the sūtra and they do not open, I will kill you. The Tibetan stood by his side.
They all watched and recited together, yet they had not finished the recitation when the lock suddenly opened with a *huá-huò* sound.
The Tibetans were astonished by this, and it turned out exactly as previously stated (as related by Zhang Suī, the Director of the Granary of Luozhou).
Pei Xuanli of Hedong served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Land at that time. During the early years of the Jiu-shi era, there were many major legal cases;
most of the investigations were conducted by newly appointed officials, and the functionaries who applied the law were particularly severe in their methods.
Once questioned, the five poisons converged upon him; of all his followers, not even one-tenth remained.

Xuānlǐ, who possessed a profound mind of right faith, had recited and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since childhood. Whenever he chanted it with a sincere heart, his shackles were broken and destroyed.

At that time, the presiding official Hou Ju (pronounced jū) was excessively stern and did not believe his words. Thinking that he had illicitly removed his shackles and fetters, he reported this matter to the judicial officer.
The officer, employing a formidable air of authority, ordered him to recite [the scripture]. When he had recited half a scroll, the shackles fell apart and came undone of their own accord.
Because of this divine efficacy, he was subsequently cleared of the charges (as related by Wei Shenming, the Prefect of Zizhou).

Wei Liqueqin of Jingzhao was a man who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. While serving in the military campaign against Liaodong, he was subsequently captured by the Goguryeo.
Several years later, he encountered an official army crossing the Liao River to punish the rebels. Seizing the opportunity during the night, he intended to join the official forces;
however, once outside the city walls, he found that the area was entirely composed of Goguryeo villages. It happened to be a dark night, and as he traveled on, he had no idea where to emerge. Thus...
He saw a bright light like a lamp, which led him away. Before long, he had arrived at the camp of the government army.

Kechin rose to the rank of Middle General (*zhonglang*) and related this miraculous sign in detail to his acquaintances, sighing in wonder at the inconceivable power of Prajñā (as recounted by Wei Shenming, the Regional Inspector of Zizhou).
Tang Yan, a native of Qi County in Zizhou, received and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From the time he first began his recitation, he never let it go in vain. In the first year of the Chang’an era, he fled and took up residence in An’uo County, Puzhou.
After twelve years had passed, he established friendly relations with dozens of local prominent families there, including Yao Quan. Upon reaching the Kai... [text continues]

In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he encountered Dou Jieshen’s son, Dou Zhi (pronounced Shi), who had been demoted from Langzhou to the position of Extraordinary Counselor of Puzhou due to the accumulated offenses of his grandfather, Dou Huai-zhen.
Because Zhi was personally acquainted with the Regional Inspector, Cui Congsu, the latter dispatched Zhi to serve as acting Magistrate of An’e County.
Yan [the author] noted that Zhi was formerly a junior official and a participant in deliberations within his own ministry.
He then conspired with his former associates to plot against Zhí, investigating and harassing prominent local families and their tenant households; because of this, they harbored resentment.

In the third year of the Kaiyuan era, Liu Fei (the second character pronounced *pǔ mò*), who had served as the Regional Inspector of Yā Prefecture, was demoted to the post of Regional Inspector of Pǔ Prefecture.
Thereupon, he accepted the accusations of the prominent families and used the pretext of Cān Fú’s escape from punishment to secretly plot his downfall. Every night, Cān would dream...
He saw a Daoist practitioner who said to him repeatedly, "Why do you not return? Why do you not return?
He did not know that the nobleman was secretly intending to harm him; fortunately, he received a warning from Renxu, the recorder of the county office.
Yan then fled to the estate of Wang Xiaogu in Fangyi County, Suzhou, where he hid in the estate. It was over eighty *li* from Puzhou. On the twelfth day...
On the twenty-third day of the month, Magistrate Liu dispatched the Judicial Officer Wang Min, leading ten laborers, to the Xiaogu Estate to arrest Yan.
Behind the estate there was only a large bamboo grove; the ground to the east, west, south, and north was entirely cleared farmland, with no weeds or brush at all.
As Yan became desperate, he fled into the bamboo grove and leaned against a tree, reciting only:
He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his voice never ceasing for a moment.

Ten men of great physical strength searched throughout the bamboo grove—crossing back and forth, from tree to tree, and from front to rear—but in the end, they did not see him and immediately returned.
Yan then fled to the city of Suizhou and stayed at the home of Zhang Xirun. Furthermore, in the first month of the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, Liu...
The Provincial Inspector (Cishi) further dispatched Zhang Guan, the Registrar of Pukang County, to deliver a letter to the Senior Secretary (Changshi) Wei Boliang with instructions to arrest Yan.
He also encountered the host, Zhang Xirun, serving as an assistant secretary. Upon returning, Zhang reported to Yan, saying:
"Today, Zhang Guan, the Registrar of Pukang County, brought a letter from Inspector Liu to the Senior Secretary; I do not know what matters are involved. When Yan heard this, he was alarmed.
He spoke thus, appearing once again filled with alarm. That night, he dreamed of a large beast that was about to come and devour him.

Startled, he suddenly rose from his seat and saw a divine king (śarīra-rakṣa) standing at the corner of the wall by the head of the bed. He looked again at Yan, who was on the bed; in an instant, the apparition vanished.
That night, at the third watch, he set out. On the seventh day of the first month, he arrived at Tongquan County and stayed there for ten days. Indeed...
I have received a letter from my host, Zhang Run, reporting that yesterday at dawn on the seventh day, the Magistrate Wei dispatched some unscrupulous men to search and seize you at Run’s house.

I trust you are aware of this. Farewell for now; may all go well. Thus I have reached my native village and am able to reach this day, entirely due to the protection of the spiritual power of Prajñā. However, Yan has a destination to reach, and the previous opportunity was not convenient.
Li saw a snake cross his path. Although it was the height of winter, this was the second time such a snake had appeared since he began reciting the sutras.
Even when entering the homes of those afflicted by illness, he has never been infected himself (Xianzhong, who was then serving as the Sima of Zizhou, personally questioned this man).
Guo Shouqiong, a native of Zhengping County in Jangzhou, was serving as the Director of Guest Relations at the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu*).

Having returned to his ancestral home, he stayed as a guest for several dozen *li* from his residence; it was only when he was about to depart with his belongings that he spoke of returning home. At that time, the sky was overcast and accompanied by a light rain.
It was said that along this road to the left, there were many tombs, and travelers would often be confused by the "ghost fires" (*guǐhuǒ*) appearing before them. Or...
In a cemetery, he fell into a pit or trench and consequently lost his soul; he passed away after several months.
Shouqiong was filled with terror and found no way out. At first, he saw ghostly fires for many tens of li, appearing as ten or twenty torches.
Suddenly he arrived, riding only a single horse and bringing no one else with him. Since he had previously recited the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, he immediately began to chant it aloud.
The flames dispersed and vanished into the vast distance. Seeing the fire recede so far, he paused his recitation for a short while;
before long, the ghostly fires gathered back together as before. He resumed his recitation, and the fire gradually moved further away. Thus, he knew that the *Prajñāpāramitā*...
As for his power, it reached both the realms of the unseen and the seen (as recounted by Guo Qiong, who at that time served as a judicial official for agricultural affairs).
The monk Shi Shenyi of Fohui Temple in Wuxuan County, Zizhou, whose secular surname was Liu (pronounced liu),
was falsely accused by a local man named Feng Zhidi in the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, claiming that Shenyi had harbored a bandit named Lu in his room.
Jin Zhu and the others subsequently fled to Luzhou to escape. There they encountered Chen Xingzhen of Dayun Monastery in Zizhou.
Because Jin Zhu had been preaching the "Fire Thieves" (Huozhai) doctrine, the Magistrate of Luzhou, Zhang She, issued a warrant to Zizhou to arrest Xingzhen.
Zizhou dispatched Zhang Lan, a local leader, to Luzhou to seize him, whereupon he was imprisoned in the Luzhou county jail. At that time, Shen... [text fragment] ...was in charge.
Yan had previously memorized the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and recited it diligently day and night for over forty days.

four li further away, there was another great city. "This is the city of hell," the two śrāmaṇeras said.
"Let us take the donor to this city to observe it. Following their teacher, they arrived there; the city was high and steep, and there was an entrance.

the agony and wailing were beyond description. Furthermore, on all four sides were iron beds and sword-trees.

He said, "The eighteen hells are all within this city. When Sengce saw this, fear arose in his heart;
he knew only to recite the Buddha’s name, constantly chanting the *Prajñāpāramitā* without ceasing. The two monks then led Sengce out of the city gate until they reached the original path.

There was a great gate blocking the entrance to the road, through which they could not pass. The two monks opened it with their mendicant staffs (*khakkhara*).
He then said to Ce, "Exert yourself and diligently cultivate merit; recite the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and do not give rise to indolence. You will surely attain longevity.
After Ce took his leave of the Master and arrived home, he regained consciousness within his body; his parents and relatives were all overcome with anxiety and fear.

He consoled him with courtesy and explained the circumstances of his ordeal. Having received permission to return home, the power of this merit caused all who heard it to rejoice, their minds becoming serene.
Through the merit of reciting this sutra and observing the fast, he exhorted and transformed all beings, causing each of them to resolve to attain enlightenment.
He recited the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day without fail, increasing his diligence even further, and subsequently attained longevity.
It is also said that Yuan Zhitong of Longcheng County in Tianshui Commandery was not yet twenty years of age when he took up the observance of the fasts and precepts;

he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and other sūtras, performing prostrations and repentances during the six periods of the day without ever missing a session. At the age of twenty—
He was immediately enrolled as a guard of the Qingde Commandery and his name was added to the military rolls. By imperial decree, he was dispatched to campaign against the Bai Man.
From his home to that destination was over ten thousand *li*. Along the way, day and night, he never ceased his ritual recitations.

Upon reaching the borders of the Southern Man, the official army was defeated and the soldiers scattered. At that time, there were more than one hundred companions who did not know where to turn; most...
He was wounded and killed. Zhìtōng was terrified and panicked; he fled in haste, but there was no way to escape.
Suddenly, five men appeared, all riding mares, positioned before and behind him. One man galloped up to Zhìtōng and told him, "Do not fear, do not be afraid!

He immediately entered it and hid himself. The Man then returned to his camp. Suddenly, two monks came to see Tong and said to him, "It is inconceivable that you, a *dānapati*, recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and pay homage and mindfulness to the Buddhas; therefore, we have been sent to rescue you.
As for those five men who were riding horses before and behind you earlier, they were all due to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*."
"It is as if they were rescuing you from enemies and bandits who would harm your body. Diligently cultivate meritorious deeds and recite and uphold the scriptures;
do not give rise to indolence. All the various benevolent spirit-kings will constantly protect you. Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended into the air and departed.
Having been unable to eat for an entire day while traveling through the mountains, he was extremely hungry and exhausted. In a short while, two youths appeared, carrying a bowl.

do not let them fall into neglect. Having spoken, the host ascended into the air and departed. Tong wept with tears of sorrow and repented from the depths of his heart. He then joined the great army;
though he passed through three successive battles, he was not wounded by even a fraction of an iron blade. Based on this cause...
These circumstances were entirely due to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Later, when the barbarians were defeated, he was released by the imperial army;
he then devoted himself single-mindedly to reciting and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, never daring to be negligent.
It is further stated: On the twenty-eighth day of the first month in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill. On the night of the eighth day of the second month, his life came to an end.
He was then led before the King. A vast multitude of followers followed behind him, all standing in line.

He passed through. When asked what meritorious deeds he had performed during his life, Tong replied to the King, saying, "Since birth, I have recited and upheld such scriptures as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*;

The messenger said, "I shall take him today. On what register do you base this pursuit? He was handed over to the presiding official, who minutely examined the records so that no one would be unjustly brought before him.

If they were not joined together, he would die immediately. The King then had a desk brought to search for them himself; indeed, it was no mistake.

He spoke to his attendants on the left and right, saying, "Bring a couch and a small table. Immediately, a golden couch and a jade table were brought from the southern wing and placed before the King.

Each fascicle was a single scroll, and he had mastered them all. Furthermore, he ordered the keeper of the archives to retrieve the registers of those who recited the scriptures and performed meritorious deeds, and to deliver them to Tong. Tong went toward the western wing to fetch them;

From the lower-middle [repository], he retrieved one scroll consisting of about ten sheets of paper. Its title was "The Ledger of Merit Compiled by Yuan Zhitong.

all were contained therein. The King said to his attendants, "The merit created by this Tong is most profound and vast indeed."
Deeply moved, he went to observe the hells to discern the karmic retributions of sin and merit. Following the command, the messengers led him out of the city.
More than five li to the northwest, there was a great city with watchtowers and defensive battlements, from which iron nets hung down.
At the gate stood four hell-wardens, their heads like those of rākṣasas, their bodies massive and tall, holding iron forks and standing to the left and right. There were two...
There were bronze dogs at both sides of the gate, their mouths spewing molten copper that flowed and poured over the prison grounds, drenching the offenders.
All those who undergo suffering enter through this gate; all eighteen hells are contained within this city.
Seeing all this clearly, his body and mind trembled with fear, and he could find no peace. He was led before the King and reported, "I have finished observing the hells."
The King said to Tong: "You have now clearly seen the retribution for your sinful and meritorious karma. You must apply yourself with diligent vigor; do not neglect your recitation and study.
Six years of life remain to you; I release you to return home. Do not harbor thoughts of regression, lest you fall into the evil realms where no one shall save you.
You must continue your recitation and never retreat from Bodhi; then I shall grant you a long life until your death in old age."
He was reborn in the Pure Land.

Initially, he recited it twice each day; after five or six years, he recited it once each day. His elder brother—

12. He was wearing mourning for his biological mother. She was one hundred and seven years old and had passed away only recently.

When the mind is defiled, all transgressions arise; when the mind is pure, all transgressions are simultaneously extinguished. Misfortune and fortune are not drawn from external things; defilement and purity must reside within the mind.

Form is not empty; by this means, bhikṣus who have transgressed the precepts suddenly cast off doubt and regret, and bodhisattvas who have broken their vows re-enter the stream of the sages.

The monk Fazang of Shishi Temple in Fu Prefecture was pure and refined in his observance of the precepts and practiced universal compassion.

In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he constructed a temple at Weichuan City in Luojiao County, consisting of more than twenty monk’s quarters and three buildings, including a Buddha hall and a lecture hall, each seven bays in length.

its adornments were inconceivable. He commissioned long sheets of paper at the Yue’ai Monastery in the capital for the transcription, and the sandalwood rollers are exquisitely crafted. When Dharmakṣema arrived during the Wude era...

In the second year, during the intercalary fifth month, he fell gravely ill. After more than twenty days had passed, he saw a person dressed in blue garments, adorned with magnificent finery, standing upon the terrace before him.
Holding a single scroll of scripture in his hand, the person addressed Dharmakara, saying:

"Throughout your entire life, you have performed great meritorious deeds, all of which were refined and sublime. Yet, you have now misappropriated the property of the Triple Gem; for this, you shall incur sin."
"Regarding the measure: the sutra I uphold is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

If you can personally compose one scroll and recite and uphold it with a sincere heart, all the sins committed throughout your entire life regarding the use of the Three Jewels' property shall be extinguished. Zang then responded accordingly.
When his sins were extinguished and his illness was cured, he immediately gave rise to a profound resolve and determinedly copied one hundred copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

He recited and maintained it without ceasing. Furthermore, he said: "Throughout my entire life, although I have performed meritorious deeds, I have never transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
For the disciples awakened by all Buddhas, there is nothing more essential than the three robes and the water flask they carry upon their person."

He immediately renounced his alms bowl and other possessions, entrusting them to the Venerable One. Knowing his illness was grave, he left instructions to his disciples and acquaintances to commission one hundred copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In the city of Śrāvastī, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, each copy was transcribed with half the characters and fully adorned.
These were then distributed to all monastics and laypeople for recitation. Through the power of the *Prajñā*, [the illness was cured].
"It is inconceivable! You have rescued and delivered all sentient beings. Having spoken these words, the Elder (Zang) passed away.
When he was brought before the King, the King inquired in detail about what meritorious deeds he had performed throughout his life. The Elder then explained: "I fashioned images of the Buddha;

He maintained the Prajñāpāramitā without ever neglecting it for even a moment. When the King heard these words, he realized that the Master’s accumulation of merit was immense and inconceivable.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to the treasury to retrieve the ledger of merits and bring it before the King. The King opened and examined it himself;
everything accorded exactly with what the Master had described, without a single error. The King said, "The Master has now constructed temples and Buddha images, and transcribed the scriptures."
Furthermore, the merit of reciting and upholding the Prajñāpāramitā is perfect and inconceivable.

Leave your teacher at the monastery and exhort all others to read and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, fully cultivating all meritorious virtues without giving rise to indolence. Your teacher shall attain long life;
when his life eventually comes to an end, he will immediately be reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions.

you must now go with us. Jia Hui asked, "How far is it from here to Mount Tai?"
"It is over three thousand *li* away. Since the journey is so long, how could one possibly reach it? The youth said, "Master, you need only close your eyes; I have my own horse.

Jia Hui saw that the Magistrate of Guzang, Murong Renguī, was sitting with his ritual tablet (hù) in hand. Jia Hui summoned him and questioned him;

His family members perceived his spirit and countenance as suddenly vacant and bewildered. In the eleventh month, he was able to recover from his ailment;
