He then said to his elder sister, "When I was a child, I suffered from an infection.
I killed a crab and took its juice to apply to the wound, which healed me. Now that I have entered the Hell of the Knife Forest, I see broken knives within my flesh."

"Seven coins. I pray that you, my sister, will extend your compassion and perform meritorious deeds to rescue me. Knowing that I am in urgent distress and cannot suddenly provide for myself, I offer these personal garments;
they are of no benefit to the deceased, yet they have not been damaged. I request that you use them. My sister did not reply.
After a while, she said, "The child has taken it away. After a long time, she spoke again, "The clothing has already arrived;
I see it on the bed. Her elder sister went to look at it and found that it was indeed the clothing she had enshrined.

She then delivered it to Master Bǎoxiàn of Jingtusi Temple and requested that he copy the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Each time a scroll was finished being copied, she would report, "One scroll has been completed."

[He wrote] "Dāo" (Sword). Having finished writing seven fascicles, he said, "The seven swords have all been drawn forth. From then until now, he has received the aid of blessings; he shall immediately go to take rebirth.
He departed after bidding farewell with tears to his elder sister and younger brother. (As told by Shen Xuanfa of Wuxing; this is the same as what was told by the monk Zhizheng of Jingtu Temple.)
The commentary states: Sentient beings are called "ordinary"; those free from craving are "sages. Only transgressions arise and perish according to whether the mind is defiled or pure.
When right mindfulness causes the mind to forget its attachments, the perverse becomes correct. Thus, the six entanglements and nine afflictions all return to the true nature.
Chapter Four: On Supernatural Powers (with preface; sixteen sections).
In antiquity, when Guāhuáng governed the realm, she severed the giant turtle to mend the heavens. Yíyì drew his bow to shoot down the sun-bird.
Upon the Xuántái Terrace, he drove the dragons of Emperor Xiàhòu; by the banks of the Yáo River, he again performed the dance of King Zhōu.

Jùn (pronounced xùn). When the Immortal Lord [Zhang Daoling] let his hidden stream gush forth fire, and Yuánfāng [Zhìyuán] concealed his shadow to divide his form—how much more so when one’s realization of the Way accords with *tathatā* (suchness), reaching the pinnacle of the peerless?
To open the stupa and transfer the celestial beings to another realm, he did so without rising from his seat.
He manifested the Wondrous Joy [Pure Land] within Jambudvīpa; his sacred and majestic achievements were so towering that they truly defy all description.
Therefore, I have recorded his most extraordinary deeds and arranged them here as the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers."
The *Record of Miraculous Efficacy of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by Xiao Yu states:

During the Liang dynasty, there was a Brahmin master named Fazang who was able to maintain the recitation of sūtras and mantras to ward off all malevolent influences. There was a junior monk who had studied the mantras for several years and claimed to have achieved mastery, believing himself capable of subduing evil spirits.
He traveled with his companion to the banks of the Yangtze River and stayed at the shrine of the Goddess of Gongting Lake.
That night, he recited various incantations. The deity of the temple subsequently came and killed him. When Huizang heard that his disciple had died, he was filled with resentment;
he went in person to the eaves of the temple shrine and stayed there overnight, reciting incantations, and consequently met his own death as well.

At that time, a monk from the same monastery who regularly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* heard that both Master Huizang and his disciples had been killed by the deity; he therefore came to the temple...
In the temple, while reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* upon his seat, he heard the sound of wind at midnight; it was exceedingly great and swift.
In a brief moment, he saw a great man whose physical form was magnificent and extraordinary, both marvelous and terrifying, with various features and eyes that flashed like lightning.
The Master sat upright in right mindfulness, reciting the sutras without ceasing. Neither fearing nor trembling, the spirit arrived before him;

it withdrew its formidable power, knelt with the right knee on the ground, joined its palms in reverence, and listened until the recitation was finished. The Master asked the spirit, "Donor, what deity are you?
You were fierce and swift when you first arrived, yet now you have become quiet. The spirit replied, "Your disciple is the deity of this Gongting Lake."
The deity was by nature fierce and violent. Upon seeing the Master reciting and studying Mahāyāna sūtras—whose merit was vast and inconceivable—he submitted and listened to the Master’s words.
The Master asked, "Since you, donor, can possess such faith and reverence, for what reason did you previously beat and kill the two monks who were reciting mantras?
The deity replied, "Those monks were unable to recite and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras. The Master said, "My younger brother..."

When the Master entered the temple, he went forward to meet them and rebuked them, using harsh words to subdue his disciples. When the two monks saw the appearance of the disciples, they were naturally struck with fear of death;

it was not that he intentionally killed the bhikṣus. When the people learned that the Master had stayed overnight in the spirit temple, they feared he would suffer the same fate as the previous two monks.
At dawn, they went together to the temple to welcome him and inquire after him; the Master remained perfectly at ease, and the people were greatly amazed.
Jiaqing asked the Master about his full knowledge [of these matters]. Consequently, many people were inspired to resolve to receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, in the first year of the Zhenguan era, Liu Bi, the Assistant Magistrate of Yilong County in Pengzhou—who had previously served as a County Sheriff in Jiangnan—[reported a vision].
Suddenly, a bird began to cry out from atop a tree in front of the house door. People said, "This is an ominous bird;
if it arrives here, the head of the household will surely be killed. Hearing this, Bi was terrified and felt helpless. During the night, he saw a monk in a dream.

He was instructed to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred times. A benevolent deity then came and pulled [the tree] out, casting it across the house and onto the middle of the main street;
yet, in the end, there was no trace of it at all. How great indeed is the power of the *Prajñāpāramitā*!

In the *Lan Yu Ling Ming Bao Shi Yi* (Supplement to the Collected Accounts of Miraculous Retribution), it is stated: Li Qian-guan of Longxi, who currently resides in Zhengzhou, was observing the three-year mourning period for his father, Fu-yin, in the fifth year of the Mingqing era.

He then drew blood to transcribe one scroll each of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Banzhou Sanmei Jing* (Heart Sūtra), as well as two scrolls of the *Sui Yuan Wangsheng Jing* (Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows). Just before he was about to go out and enter [the bathhouse], he performed a ritual bath once.
Suddenly, a strange fragrance was perceived within the monastery, exceedingly intense and pervasive.

Those living nearby all went to observe it, and there were none who did not offer words of praise (I, Yu Ling, once passed through Zhengzhou and heard this account from a relative; it was also transmitted by a friend).
It is further said that in a village twenty li west of Jiyin County in Caozhou, there was a vihāra.

In the tenth month of winter in the second year of the Longshuo era, a wild fire suddenly broke out with extraordinary intensity. It reached the vihāra and leaped across it, spreading even to the monks' quarters;
all the thatched huts were consumed by the flames until nothing remained, except for a single copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The scroll remains as solemn and intact as before (as related by Yuan Hui, Military Aide to the Governor of Caozhou). It further states:
During the Mingqing era, Sun Shou, a native of Pingzhou, was hunting along the seashore when he saw a wild fire blazing fiercely, consuming all the grasses and trees.
There was, however, only one thicket of lush vegetation that was not scorched by the flames; he suspected there was something within this grass.
The beast then attempted to burn it with fire, but in the end, he could not set it alight. Shou was greatly perplexed by this and entered the undergrowth to search;
there he saw a case containing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Beside it, he also saw a dead monk whose complexion remained unchanged.
This is why fire does not spread and consume [the house]. (Sun Shou personally witnessed this and recounted it.
It is further said that Sima Qiaoqing of Henei, formerly a Judicial Rectifier at the Ministry of Justice, was stingy yet pure, prudent, and possessed of ultimate integrity.

During the Yonghui era, while serving as the Head of the Revenue Bureau in Yangzhou, he encountered the mourning period for his mother. While observing the rites of mourning, he emaciated himself through grief and pierced his chest to draw blood, with which he transcribed [the scriptures].
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Not long after, two stalks of *zhī* grass grew upon Mount Lu.

After nine days, they had grown to a length of one chi and eight cun. They had green stems and crimson caps; each day they dripped one sheng of juice. Beside them, food appeared sufficiently for consumption.

Its flavor was as sweet as honey. Once exhausted, it grew again. This occurred four times in succession. (Several colleagues of mine recounted this to me and requested that I record it. I have also recorded it in detail in the *Xiaozizhuan*.)
Yáng Tǐjī, a Grand Master of the Middle Grade (Dàzhōng Dàfū), was a native of Jīngzhào. In the first year of the Dàjí era, he served as the Regional Secretary (Chángshǐ) of Ráo Prefecture.

By imperial decree, he was concurrently appointed as the Grand Commissioner (Dàshǐ) for the Silver Mountain to oversee the extraction of silver. As for the silver mines and the laborers employed there—
The artisan’s movement surpassed that of ten thousand men. The neighboring commoners collectively established a marketplace there. Within this market, there were no tiled houses at all;

everyone used thatched screens and mats as dwellings, with their eaves and corridors joined together. One night, a house suddenly caught fire, and the buildings within the market were completely consumed, leaving nothing behind.
Only the house in the center was not reached by the flames; its structure remained almost entirely intact.

The patrol inspector questioned him as to how this had come about. He replied that there was an elderly man in his household who constantly recited and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
By the power of the *Prajñā*, fire could not burn it; throughout the entire prefecture, there was no one who was not struck with wonder.
The monk Shi Qingxu of Huiyi Temple in Zizhou was of the Tang clan by secular surname. By nature he was stern and resolute; from his youth, he had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇitā Sūtra*.

In the tenth month of the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, at Sanzong Mountain north of Lingyan Temple in Qizhou, he made a profound vow with deep resolve for the sake of all sentient beings suffering in the three miserable realms, and began to uphold the [Sūtra].
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he made a vow that all sentient beings might quickly attain liberation from suffering.
From the third day of the tenth month until the sixth, seven-headed deer suddenly came to listen to the sutra; whenever the recitation began, they would immediately come and lie prostrate to listen.
Having finished reciting, he departed. When the entire recitation was concluded, he did not return again.

On the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, Seng Qingxu was sitting upright and reciting a sutra at Mount Sandong in Lingyan Temple, Qizhou, when the sun was setting.
Suddenly, as if in a dream, he no longer saw his dwelling, house, mountains, or rivers.
At the stone wall, he saw only a single city that resembled the city of Zizhou.

The monk entered through the eastern gate and, upon reaching a bridge, saw a man at a checkpoint who was a native of the east of the mountains. He then proceeded out through the western gate for about five or six li.
He also saw a city on the left side of the road. The city was five li in length and breadth.
The monk stepped off the path and arrived at the eastern gate of the city; the gate was so narrow that it could barely accommodate a single person entering.
The monk asked the gatekeeper, "Do you know when the Great King will release the sentient beings suffering in hell? The keeper replied, "Yesterday at noon. [This occurred] in Qizhou.
At Insan Temple there was a Zen master, holding a monk’s staff, about seventy years of age, who came before the King and said to him:
"There is a visiting monk who, for the sake of sentient beings suffering in the three miserable realms, recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*."
"Does Your Majesty know? When will the Heavenly King cease and release these sentient beings who are suffering in hell?
The King replied to the master, saying, "I already knew this. Tomorrow at noon, I shall release a small portion of those whose offenses are light for you, Master.
The gatekeeper said to the monk, "Master, depart at once; please do not speak further. The monk then turned back and departed.
He entered through the western gate and arrived before the door of an inn. Ahead, he saw a melon about the size of a bowl; he broke it into two pieces and ate one, leaving the other behind.
When he reached the place where the shop was located, the shopkeeper asked the monk where he had obtained this melon and requested a piece.
Having received the melon, the man ate it and remarked, "It is only in the tenth month that such a delicious fruit appears."
Before he had finished speaking, he suddenly saw a vast multitude of people entering through the western gate of the city.
There were many women and few men; those wearing mourning clothes of hempen cloth were numerous, while those in festive attire were rare.
They approached the monk’s seat and each paid their respects, seeking the master’s deliverance. The monk replied, "We have never known one another before. Why [have you come]?"
He rescued him. Later, three young servants also came to pay their respects. Having received the Master’s rescue, the monk asked them, "Whose children are you?
Your complexions are so pale and your appearances so haggard. Where have you come from? Your robes are all new;
for what reason are you in such a state? They replied, "We are the family servants of the Xuanzong Temple. We were thieves..."
He observed his household’s grain and wheat, prepared wine, and purchased meat, unaware of the quantity. He was brought before King Yama for interrogation;

it had been five years since he last passed through this world, and he had not known even a single drop of broth or water. His robe was one he had worn while alive, which he began to wear only after death.
As he was being interrogated, his robe was stripped from him and hung upon the head of the Nàhé (Naihe) tree. Thus he obtained a new one. Having finished speaking, he took his leave.
The efficacy [of this practice] was thus proven.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, while Qingxu was at Mount Santong in Qizhou, a wind suddenly arose from the east toward evening.
From afar, he saw a wild fire burning the mountains; it was situated at a distance of approximately...
After traveling more than ten li, when it reached the hour of midnight, the fire gradually drew near until it was about one hundred paces from where the monk sat.
The monk’s heart was struck with alarm; he recited the sutras, called upon the Buddha's name, and chanted the Eleven-faced Dharani.
When the fire was only about fifty paces from his dwelling, a sudden whirlwind arose and the flames were extinguished of their own accord. This continued until the first watch of the night.
Suddenly it flared up again. The monk took a broom and beat out the fire, so that it did not burn. Within less than ten paces of the house, the fire extinguished itself;
within those ten paces, the thatch and the eaves (pronounced *yán*) were level, yet there remained a heap of disordered grass.
The distance from the ridgepole did not exceed several feet; by the time it reached them, the tangled weeds and thatch were all reduced to ashes and embers.
Only the bedroom escaped the fire. On its northeast side, both the eaves were consumed by the flames. One can truly know that the power of Prajñā is inconceivable.
In the second month of the first year of the Dengdui era, the monk Qingxu came to Mount Tu.
He usually recited the sutra no more than twice, yet his waist and spine were so painful that he could not endure them. Before the Buddha, the monk then made this vow:
"Tonight, I shall sit in the full lotus posture and, for the sake of all sentient beings, recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* until it is completed five times."

One must recite until the full number is reached before finally ceasing. Even if the pain is such that it feels like being cut or pierced, one must ultimately complete the count, using death as the limit.
When the recitation reaches the third round, the joints and bones feel as if they are being torn apart. When the recitation reaches the fourth round, there are beings fighting inside the Buddha hall;
their voices are like those of water buffaloes and wild beasts contending for strength as they fight, and the Buddha hall itself shakes. When the recitation reaches the fifth round—
All his various pains were completely healed. He raised his eyes and looked around; everything was bright and clear, yet he could not see the Buddha hall or the lecture hall at all.
He only perceived himself sitting upright in mid-air, and the great earth was level and even, without any high or low places.

When his companions came and called out to him, he heard their voices from the void but saw no one. Only when his companions reached out their hands and pulled him up did he finally [regain consciousness].
Upon awakening, the spiritual power of Prajñā is beyond all description.
In the eighth month of the second autumn of the first year of the Shengli era, while the monk Qingxu was in Yuzhou, he went to pay homage at Fawang Temple.
He saw that within the Śarīra stupa, the entirety of the Buddhist canon was enshrined; furthermore, the four sides of the stupa had no doors. Thereupon...
A flock of pigeons entered the interior of a śarīra-stūpa. Seeing a monk enter the stūpa to prostrate, they all flew away at once.
When the monk had finished his liturgical repentance and sat within the entrance of the stūpa, a single pigeon descended from the air and flew straight into the monk’s embrace;

it passed over his left and right shoulders (shàn, pronounced jiān), then reached his head, circled him three times below, and then soared high into the sky. Even a bird thus understands how to show reverence.
Those who uphold this sutra are also rare among men; one must exert oneself.
In the intercalary fourth month of the third year of the Chang’an era, the monk Qingxu went to Wuzhen Temple in the Southern Mountains of Lantian County to observe the summer retreat.
At the Chan Hall of the Upper Ward of that temple, there was formerly no spring water, so everyone had to fetch it from the bottom of a mountain stream.

The water was more than ten *li* away. The monks of the meditation hall considered it a hardship. Master Kāṅ-tsang of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, together with the three administrators, deliberated on the matter.
The community requested that he pray for a spring. The monk replied to the assembly, saying, "This is a difficult task involving fire.
The disciples all said, "Since you, Master, have spent the summer retreat in this seat, please apply your mind to recitation and pray for the sake of the monastery."
I had intended to abandon my cultivation of the Way, yet I did not wish to offer excuses. Since I could not bear to go against the hearts of the multitude, I sought a secluded place for recitation;
however, both the upper and lower quarters of the Chan monastery were already full. There was only one Maitreya Pavilion in the center.

It was closed and constantly locked; no one dared to open it. When the monk saw it was closed, he immediately summoned the *zhisui* (steward) for consultation, wishing to open this pavilion so that he might perform recitations within it.
The master of the house, along with the visiting monks, said to the monk, "Do not go toward this pavilion."
In the pavilion there was a black snake, as large as an alms bowl and two zhang in length, which constantly guarded this pavilion, fearing it might harm the master.
The monk reported: "In Jiangnan there is the spirit of Gongting Lake; his body is several li long and he possesses mastery over transformations.
He is also a great serpent capable of summoning torrential rain and driving winds, yet even he comes to submit and take refuge. How much more so, then, this smaller one?"

"What need is there for further words? The monk immediately requested the key and opened the door; taking a torch, he entered directly. He saw no objects at all, but only smelled the stench of snakes.
With right mindfulness, the monk burned incense and made this invocation: "I, your disciple, have heard that great-bodied beings guard this pavilion.
I suspect they may be past worthies and sages, or perhaps mountain dragons and various deities. Today, your disciple [turns toward them...]"

Within this pavilion, he recited with single-minded devotion, petitioning for a spring for the Shangfang Chan Monastery. He prayed that all the deities would provide protection and ensure there was no cause for fear.
As he listened to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, [the deity] bestowed upon his disciple a small spring to supply the Shangfang Chan Monastery.
Thereupon, he continued his recitation with utmost sincerity, remaining seated for three days and three nights. His eyes—
Without blinking his eyes (the character for "eyelash" is pronounced "jié"), he saw three women within the range of his mental vision at the northwest of the Maitreya Pavilion.
On the slope of the mountain, they were gouging the earth with knives; suddenly, they vanished. When dawn broke, he proceeded toward the northeast.
Standing by a mountain stream, he closed his eyes and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereupon he saw a stream of water flowing from the spot where the women had dug the earth with their knives.
The monk passed by him and went on. After three or five days, he saw the monk clearly and constantly, yet he did not yet consider it a sign of truth.
He continued reciting without ceasing. After another two days, the vision became increasingly clear. The monk then moved toward the spot where the woman had been seen digging the ground with a knife;
as he recited the sutra there, he closed his eyes and again saw water flowing out from behind him. After another three days, the monk...
He then took his staff and pried it open; pushing aside the leaves, he saw a patch of damp earth about two chi in diameter.
He dug at it with a hoe and discovered a vein of water, forming a small pit capable of holding more than a stone’s weight.
As he recited the sutra with utmost sincerity for a fifth time, the water in the pit suddenly filled to the brim. He drew it toward the meditation courtyard.
By providing for the needs of the multitude, one knows that there is nothing the Sage does not respond to; when moved by conditions, he necessarily penetrates them.
Thus, it is truly believed that the merit of Prajñā is beyond all praise.
At the end of the third month in the fourth year of the Chang’an era, the monk Qingxu went to Shaolin Temple on Mount Shaoshi to observe the summer retreat.
The meditation hall of that temple was situated to the west. On the mountain to the north of that hall, there was a Buddha hall where none of the monks dared to go after nightfall.
There was a Vinaya master who, however, would go there at night to recite the Vinaya, and he heard voices from the air.
He said, "Master, you must leave quickly; if you delay, it will bring harm upon you.

By the end of the second watch, he had not yet managed to escape, when a divine general pierced his ribs with the point of a sword (pronounced *xiào*). He then descended the mountain and returned home.
At noon the following day, the Vinaya Master passed away. Less than half a year later, there was a junior monk who specialized in maintaining the fire at the head of the altar.
The Master of the *Gang* Dhāraṇī had his disciples test the power of the incantation together. A junior monk immediately performed the ritual and recited the spell over a tree;
the tree’s many branches were simultaneously bound together, or its numerous limbs were all bent down at once. Seeing this miraculous efficacy, the assembly consulted with the junior monk.
There was an old hall in the upper quarters where no one dared to stay overnight; since the Master held the divine incantation, they felt he would dare to stay within it.
He asked whether he had been reciting the mantras there overnight. The junior disciple replied, "Even at a place ten thousand times more powerful than this, [the deity] was already subdued;
this is but a minor matter and hardly worth mentioning. The junior disciple then solemnly took up the incense burner and went there to recite the mantras.
Relying on the power of his spells, he subdued that deity. That night, the deity manifested its form, seized him by both feet, and flung him—
He headed toward the bottom of a mountain stream. For seven days he lost his voice, and for more than half a year his spirit remained diminished.

A virtuous monk from Shaolin, having heard that while Qingxu was in the capital, he had requested water at Wuzhen Temple and simultaneously subdued a great serpent—both of which were divinely efficacious—said to the monk:
"Master, you who uphold the scriptures possess great spiritual power. I request that you perform a small ritual."
He sent someone to inform them, who reported back, saying, "Virtuous One, you wish to send us to a pure and secluded place; for what ritual purpose?

The assembly replied in unison, "In the upper quarters there is a Buddha hall where no one has dared to stay overnight for some time. Can you, Master, go there alone to perform recitations and stay the night?
The monk replied, "This is a place where honored guests of three generations have resided; it is precisely the abode of the Master."

Regarding the place where the monks rely for their residence: how was it that they could not find it? Those monks immediately prepared fragrant oil and went there to perform recitations for two nights and three days, yet they saw nothing at all.

The monks asked the monks of the Chan monastery, "The [monks] from □□□ have been gone for two or three days; where have they all gone? The monks of the Chan monastery replied, "To the Upper Quarters."

Inside the Buddha hall, he stayed overnight and engaged in recitation. The virtuous ones (mahātmans) urgently summoned him, but because they arrived at different times, he was struck and killed by a deity.
When the assembly came together and called out, "Master, come forth! the monk replied, "I have no cause for concern whatsoever.
The disciples all said, "The Master is no different from ordinary people; we are of one kind. Why do you wish to harm yourself here?"
He replied, "I fear nothing regarding the myriad affairs of this world; Virtuous One, simply return. When the first watch of the night was nearly over, the spirit arrived.
To the east of the Buddha hall, it let out a thunderous roar, sounding like the hurling of dozens of tails, its noise shaking the air.
The monk immediately lit a fire and went out to look, but all was silent and nothing was seen. His hair stood on end, and he immediately recited the Eleven-faced [Avalokiteśvara] mantra.
While reciting the Avalokiteśvara Dhāraṇī and circumambulating the Buddha hall once, there was the sound of water buffaloes fighting within the hall, and the image also shook.
When he recited the dhāraṇī seven times, the sound became even more violent; they continued to bellow and roar, echoing through the valleys and shaking the mountains.
He then stood upright before the Buddha hall and contemplated, not daring to enter. Suddenly, he again reflected: "Why am I here? It is not right."
He was able to subdue it. As he pressed down his mind and entered [meditation], the sound grew even more intense; even the lamps within the hall appeared to go out.
Since the incantation had no effect, he then recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon reciting it once, the sound gradually diminished; by the third recitation, the sound ceased entirely. When dawn arrived, all was silent and peaceful. Thus, one knows the power of the *Prajñā*.

Inconceivable! On the eleventh day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Qushen era, Tripitaka Master Yijing and Preceptor Jing of Qizhou submitted a memorial requesting that Qingxu enter the palace to pray for snow.
After twenty-one days, although a small amount fell, it was not yet sufficient for all. An imperial edict was issued.
The Emperor’s words were clear and detached. He said, "Master, although your prayers have not been granted as you wished, you may choose whichever monastery you prefer to reside in.
The monk, regretting that his petition had failed to accord with the Sage's will, replied to the imperial decree:

"Truly, I am not pleased. When the Great Virtues witnessed this response, they all turned pale. [The Emperor declared: "Since the Master has thus provoked the Imperial Majesty, he must be handed over for legal punishment. The decree was issued.

He further said: "When it snowed and rained, the Master was immediately presented with two hundred pieces of variegated silk and granted the rank of the Fifth Grade, and appointed as the administrator of Jianfu Temple.
What was the Master’s intention? He did not seem pleased. I asked him why, and he replied: 'I am fortunate to have been favored by Your Majesty's thoughts and commissioned to pray for snow and rain.
I only regret that above I did not cover the Heavenly Mind, and below I did not fulfill the hopes of the people.'"
My foolish sincerity is in vain; it does not satisfy Your Majesty’s holy mind. Day and night I am filled with apprehension and know only how to await my punishment.
That I have been undeservedly favored by Your Imperial Grace makes me feel no joy. The Imperial Edict states: "Let the Master be released for a time to go outside and perform recitations.

You must continue to offer prayers. Should snow or rain suddenly fall, you must immediately submit a report. Consequently, I submitted this memorial: "This time there has been no rain or snow; let this be for the sake of all beings."
The sentient beings burned their fingers. Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "I summoned the Master to receive my offerings; how can you now send the Master here to suffer?
Moreover, these are the physical remains of one's parents—how could they be mutilated or injured? The Master must certainly not allow himself to be harmed in such a reckless manner."

Having finished his meal, he took leave of the Emperor and departed. He immediately went to the waterfall at Tantou (the "tu" pronounced as "zhiyou") in the Southern Mountains to pray for snow and rain.
Although snow did fall, it ultimately could not satisfy his wishes. He moved again to the Anle Buddha Hall in Suqu Village, where he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
After another seven days, a light amount of snow fell, yet it still did not satisfy his wishes. Thereupon, he...

He made a vow to burn two joints of his finger. After one day and one night had passed, while the burning was not yet complete, clouds suddenly gathered from all four directions, and snow and rain fell intermingled.
The assembly was all struck with astonishment and wonder. It ceased only on the second day.

The common people and elders submitted a joint petition wishing to report the matter to the throne, suggesting that it be discussed together with the Tripitaka Master at Jianfu Monastery and other locations. Qingxu [arrived] at the city yesterday.
He burned two finger-joints as an invocation for rain and snow within the Dharma-realm. When he had completely consumed both joints, everyone watched together;

all the bone ash remains visible even now. This morning, when the villagers, both old and young, wished to apply medicinal ointment to them, those two finger-joints were restored to their former state.
The Tripitaka Master then said, "This matter is difficult to believe; it does not accord with human nature. He is..."
"Ordinary monks who have not yet attained the stage of Arhat—how could their burned fingers be restored to life once they have been completely consumed?
Since they do not belong to the ranks of the sages, such a thing is impossible. You must immediately inform the local magistrates and authorities that this is nothing but a demonic delusion;
it will bring harm instead of benefit and will only lead to the punishment of the elders. This is not merely a deception of the common folk, but is also a slander [against the Sangha]."
Deceiving His Majesty, when the monastic community heard this, their lack of faith increased all the more.

Seeing that the multitude had begun to slander him, the monk entered the ritual hall once again and invoked the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the worthy sages, saying: "For the sake of the sentient beings of the dharma-realm, your disciple..."
He burned his finger to pray for snow, and the various devas and nāga kings responded by causing snow to fall at that very moment.
Furthermore, he caused the fingers of his disciples that had been burned to be consumed by fire and then regrow. Consequently, they all raised slanderous words and failed to cultivate pure faith;
having misled the fourfold assembly, they fell into hell. His disciple now makes a renewed vow to recite the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, praying that within two days his finger may be restored.
It fell off. When the second day arrived, he redoubled his recitations and prayers; the two joints of his regrown finger fell off once more.
Seeing the fingers fall away, the assembly again raised slanderous words, saying, "This master burned them alive at that time, and now they have only just fallen off.
The monk then informed the assembly, "Let us go to the place where we previously prayed for snow south of the city; there I shall tend the wound so that it may grow back. They did as he said.

"Do you understand? The crowd replied in unison, "This master seems to have fallen into a mad illness; he constantly utters slanderous words. They then went to the south of the city to tend to his sores.
He recited his prayers without ceasing. By the fifteenth day, another joint and a half had grown on his fingers, and his fingernails had also emerged.
Among those who saw this, there were none who were not struck with wonder. They all said, "This is not at all strange."
If a practitioner of the Way possesses demonic arts, one thereby knows the power of Prajñā, which those of the Two Vehicles do not know.
When ordinary people hear of this, they are all able to give rise to slander.

In the second year of the Jinglong era, Qingxu first returned to his hometown. On the night of the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Taiji era, the waters of the East River surged;
at that time, the monk was staying at Huoyi Temple, and the water flowed directly into the temple grounds.
The assembly of monks each gathered their own clothing and belongings. In that monastery hall, there was a small upper chamber;

all the garments were placed upon it, whereupon he immediately lit a lamp and sat cross-legged. With single-minded concentration and right mindfulness, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
After a long while, he heard the sound of water entering the room. He took a torch to look, but not a single drop of water was to be found. His...
All the other rooms were flooded with water; those who heard of or witnessed this were not merely one person. The majestic power of the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to describe in detail.
Chen Wenjian was a native of Qi County in Zizhou. He held the rank of Qiduwei (Commandant of Cavalry). Every time he was in the prefecture...

In the hall at the head of the city gate, he constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, vowing to do so eighty-four thousand times for the sake of his parents, grandparents, and others;

he soon completed this recitation. The Regional Inspector Yuan Shenyi was summoned to the capital and ordered Wen Jian to recite the *Prajñā Sūtra* five thousand times; Jian immediately recited it for him until Shenyi arrived.
Upon arriving at the capital, all were granted exoneration.
There was a man named Chen De from Tongsan County who made his living by transcribing scriptures. Suddenly, he fell ill with a rash and was summoned by the authorities of the underworld.
He saw a platform being constructed underground and asked, "What kind of platform is this? The officials of the underworld replied, "This is..."
The Prajñā Platform: When Chen Wenjian was about to arrive, he constructed this platform to await him. His virtue restored Su, who recounted these events in detail.
News of this spread far and wide, and people vied with one another to uphold the *Prajñā* (as related by Master Huirong of Lingrui Temple on Mount Niutou).
Bei Tingguang of Zhaojun served as the *simā* (vice-commandant) of Dezhou. He had deep faith in the law of cause and effect.
Whenever he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, there was always a circular halo visible before his eyes. As his recitation became more diligent, the light gradually grew larger;

when his recitation was sparse, the light would immediately diminish. Thus he knew that the *Prajñāpāramitā* had responded to him in secret, and that it was through the penetration of his sincere devotion.
The encomium says: How great is this spiritual power! It is inconceivable. A lotus supports the Dharma-seat; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. The earth transforms through supernormal powers;
the heavens open to reveal the Sage’s pool. It is neither concentration nor wisdom—how could it be attained by either?
