Now, supreme achievement is no achievement; it acts yet has no sovereign. Supreme virtue is no virtue; it accomplishes yet does not dwell therein. Thus, the nine concentrations...
The four dhyānas involve entering that which has nothing to enter; the three emptinesses and six perfections involve practicing that which has nothing to practice.
It is boundless and infinite, neither form nor name, unstained and non-abiding. Even the accumulation of bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot equal the merit of these four verses.
How great indeed are its divine power and holy virtue! Therefore, this chapter on merit and virtue is composed to encourage those who come after.
The *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by Xiao Yu states:

In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenchang, a Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Treasury, died; however, his heart remained warm. At that time, his family members did not dare to bring him in for burial.
He was taken by others to the presence of King Yama, who questioned Zhao Chang, saying: "Throughout your entire life, what meritorious deeds have you performed?"
Chang reported to the King, saying, "Throughout my life I have been poor and possessed no other merit; I have focused my mind solely on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon hearing these words, the King joined his palms in reverence and praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!

To uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* brings forth merit that is exceedingly great and inconceivable. The King then spoke to the official Chang who had been holding him, saying, "You must investigate this thoroughly."
[The official] corrected him, saying, "Do not bring the wrong one. The official in charge of the records consulted with the King, who confirmed that the person had indeed brought the wrong one.
This individual was further destined to remain for twenty-odd more years. Upon hearing these words, the King examined his own actions and found no error.

He immediately said to Chang, "Go with the messenger and retrieve the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from within the treasury. He then dispatched a man to lead Chang southwest for about five [li].
Six *li* outside, he arrived at the repository of the scriptures. There he saw several dozen buildings, which were exceedingly magnificent and elegant. The volumes of scripture filled them entirely;
their golden rollers and precious cases were so richly adorned and beautifully decorated that they could not be described in words.

Chang then single-mindedly joined his palms, closed his eyes, and reached out by chance to draw one volume. Its size was just like that of the *Prajñāpāramitā* he had previously recited. As for its title and merits:
[Song-Mu+Qu] was the first. Chang then became apprehensive, fearing it might not be the Prajñāpāramitā; he sought out the messenger to request an exchange, but the latter refused.
Chang opened it and saw that it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. He brought it before the king. The king ordered one person to hold the scripture in the west while Chang stood in the east.
The king commanded his attendants to fetch a couch and a desk made of the seven precious gems and had Chang sit upon them to recite the scripture facing west;
he did so with complete fluency. At that time, the king instructed Chang to return home, further entrusting him with the following charge: "You must uphold and maintain [this teaching]."
Regarding this sutra, take care not to let it fall into neglect or omission. Furthermore, you must exhort all people to read and recite it.
Then, have one person lead Chang out through the southern gate. There, he saw Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty confined within a room to the east of the gate.
The Emperor immediately called out to Chang, saying, "You are a native of my own kingdom. You have come here for a short time, and I must speak with you. Chang then approached him.
He bowed twice before Emperor Wu. Emperor Wu asked, "Do you recognize me? Chang replied, "Your servant formerly served as a guard to Your Majesty.
Emperor Wu said to Chang, "You are my old acquaintance. You may return home and speak on my behalf to the Emperor of Sui.
My various offenses have all been cleared, but only the matter of the destruction of the Buddha-dharma remains unresolved. It should—"
At that time, Yuan Song of the Right Guard taught me to extinguish the Buddha-dharma. I have pursued Yuan Song until now without success; for this reason, it remains unresolved.
Chang asked Emperor Wu, "Where is Yuan Song? He cannot be apprehended. The Emperor said, "As for this Yuan Song, he is one outside the three realms;
he is not under the jurisdiction of King Yama, so he cannot be apprehended. You should return [to your practice]."
I quickly requested a small measure of merit from Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
After traveling for a short distance, Chang went outside the southern gate and saw a person with only their hair protruding from a large heap of excrement. Chang asked the guide, "What is this?
The guide replied, "This is Bai Qi, the general of Qin. For unjustly burying alive the soldiers of Zhao, his punishment remains incomplete even now. Upon returning home, Chang obtained [the merit].

After he had recovered, his ailment gradually subsided over the course of three days. He presented a detailed report to Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, who immediately issued an edict that all monasteries throughout the realm should observe a three-day fast on behalf of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Emperor further commanded that this record be included in the official history of the Sui dynasty.
It is further said that during the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenruo of Yongzhou died and seven days passed. When his family was about to place him in the coffin for burial, he contracted one leg;
consequently, they did not bury him and he immediately revived. He spoke, saying that while dead he had seen King Yama, who questioned him.
"What meritorious deed did you perform while alive? He replied, "I upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King said, "Excellent, excellent! This is the foremost merit among all merits. Although you have cultivated such merit, nevertheless, show me the place where you suffer retribution.
Then, he had one man lead him northward for several dozen paces until they reached a wall with a hole in it, which separated them.
Inside a hole in the wall was a person who reached out a hand and seized him, pulling him through with extreme hardship. Outside the wall, he saw the great hells:
cauldrons of boiling water and glowing coals, mountains of knives and trees of swords, copper pillars and iron beds. The suffering of the sinners there was inconceivable.
There were also fowl, pigs, sheep, geese, and ducks, which demanded their debts from him according to his past lives. They spoke to him, saying:
"I shall not fail your life. The chickens and others replied, "On such a year, month, and day, you shall go together with a person from such a province to divide my head and feet;
each of you shall eat them. Only when you hear what these animals have said and witnessed will you know that this is no falsehood."
He also recounted the places where he had slaughtered and eaten animals in the past; the man could do nothing but recite the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and repent his transgressions.

The pigs, sheep, chickens, and ducks did not dare speak further. When the person being led was about to return to the king’s presence, he informed the king, saying, "I have finished observing the place where I am to undergo punishment.
At that time, the king gave him a bowl of iron nails and ordered him to eat them, all of which were long nails.
Five nails were driven into his head, crown, hands, and feet; he was released only when they were all removed.

Although he subsequently recovered from his coma, he continued to suffer from headaches as well as pain in his hands and feet. However, the areas where he suffered gradually healed. From that time onward...
Diligent and tireless, he upheld the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Whenever he encountered relatives or acquaintances, he would invariably exhort them to uphold this sutra.
Later, while on official business, he arrived at a post station and lay down for a brief rest;
as if about to fall asleep, he dreamed that a woman dressed in blue clothing came rushing toward him and cried out, "Save me! Save me! Startled awake, he immediately called out:
The station master asked, "Did you not kill another living being for me? The station master replied, "Just now I was about to kill a small sheep for you.
He asked, "What color is it? and was told, "It is a blue ewe. [The other] said, "If you will release it quickly, do not kill it."

He nevertheless paid the price to redeem the sheep and released it to live out its natural lifespan. Is this not because of the sincere response brought about by upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*?
The *Láng Yúlíng Míngbào Shíyí* states: "The Dharma Master Xīxuán of Puguang Temple practiced asceticism from his youth and constantly..."

He took the lecturing and reciting of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as his primary vocation. In the eleventh month of winter in the second year of the Longshuo era, he sat upright within the monastery and passed away, remaining solemn and motionless.
When the Emperor heard of this, he praised him and issued an edict stating: "The monk Xiqian of Puguang Monastery has cultivated his virtuous conduct with purity;
both monastics and laypeople revered him. He has suddenly attained parinirvāṇa while sitting upright, causing the assembly of Śākya disciples to feel as if their main beam had collapsed."

It is appropriate that he be buried with the rites of the third rank, and a division of the *guchui* (drum and wind ensemble) should be provided. The men and women of the entire city gathered to watch, as numerous as a marketplace.
(The remaining instructions shall be seen in the section concerning the meeting with various virtuous monks and friends in the capital.)
It is further said: Yiwei Gaocun was the grandson of Qigong Ying, the *puye* (vice-president of the Secretariat) of the Sui dynasty, and the son of Cishi Biao-ren.
In the second year of the Longshuo era, while in Chang’an, he emerged through the Shunyi Gate and suddenly encountered two ghosts, each riding a horse.
They said to him, "The King has summoned you. He replied, "I am but a living man," and did not believe them; he then spurred his horse to avoid them.
The two demons galloped again to seize him, ordering one rider to go to the gate of Puguang Temple to wait. They then said to each other, "Do not let him enter the temple;
once he has entered, we fear he will be impossible to capture. After he had passed through, they continued to escort him toward the west.
They arrived at both Kaishan and Huichang Temples, where they treated him in the same manner. There were brothers who had left the household life at Huadu Temple, and [the demons] intended—
He went toward the temple gate, but the ghosts would not allow him to enter. He then seized them;
Zhen struck one ghost once, whereupon the ghosts became enraged and dragged him from his horse, causing him to fall into a swoon.

A monk at the temple gate saw that he had fallen from his horse alone, with no one else by his side, so he carried him into the room where his brothers stayed. After one night, he finally regained consciousness.
After he had regained consciousness, he recounted his experience in detail, saying: "I was led before the king. The king said, 'This man does not yet deserve to come here;
let him undergo this living punishment. Because he had previously slandered the Sangha, they were ordered to plow his tongue.
His tongue then grew several inches long, yet it suffered no injury. When people asked him, "For what reason did your tongue grow so long without being damaged? he replied: [as follows].
He said, "Because I had previously recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it was unable to cause me harm. After one night, the symptoms ceased.
Later, he again placed his hand toward his mouth as if swallowing something; in an instant, a red streak emerged from beneath his collar and flowed into his abdomen.
Thereupon, he collapsed stiffly and died while crying out. This occurred several times a day. People—
When asked the reason for this, he replied, "In my youth, I stole temple fruit and snacks; that is why I swallowed iron balls.

He did this for twenty days before ceasing. Thereafter, he devoted himself to ascetic practice and has not consumed alcohol or meat until the present day (the rest was related by him when he came to the capital to take the imperial examination, as I heard with my own ears).
It is further said that at Shibi Temple in Bingzhou there was an elderly monk whose practice consisted of meditation and recitation. He was diligent and refined in his conduct.
Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, a dove built a nest upon the pillar of his dwelling and raised two fledglings. Whenever the monk had leftover food, [he would give it to them].
He constantly went to the nest to feed them. Although the pigeon chicks gradually grew older, their wings and feathers were not yet fully formed;
as they attempted to fly together, they fell to the ground and perished. The monk collected and buried them all.

After ten days had passed, the monk suddenly dreamed of two small children at night who said to him, "We children previously committed some minor transgressions, and consequently received the bodies of pigeons. Recently, we heard of the Dharma Master..."
Having recited the Lotus Sūtra and the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, and having heard the sublime Dharma, they have obtained human bodies.
Your children are now being conceived as males in the household of such-and-such a surname in a certain village, some ten-odd *li* from the side of this monastery;
beyond ten months, they shall be born. The monk then went to visit them at the appointed time and saw that a woman of this family was simultaneously [pregnant].
He gave birth to two sons. Consequently, he performed the *pūrṇamāsa* ceremony for them; when the monks called out "Pigeon-child" (*kapotaka*), both children responded in unison, saying, "Yes.

After more than a year had passed, they began to speak. (Jia Zhi Zhong previously served as a *boshi* in Bingzhou and was later transferred to the post of *sihu* in Xi州. He related this to Yu Ling. Later, when inquiries were made in Bingzhou, all confirmed it to be an authentic account.)
Yu Chang, Duke of Qinchang and former Governor of Qingzhou, once served as the Registrar of the Jing Prefecture.
Every time it reached the hour after the first watch, his breathing would become faint and labored, and sweat would pour from his entire body; by the time of cockcrow, he would recover completely.
He suffered no further pain, yet he felt his physical frame grow emaciated and his spirit weary and distressed. Those around him marveled at this and questioned him, but the Duke remained silent.
This was not permitted. Lady Liu requested that a physician be summoned, but the Duke did not allow it. The Lady then secretly asked him the reason for this.
He replied, "I have no other ailment; I simply suffer from presiding over legal affairs by day and judging matters of the underworld at night.

The Lady then inquired about matters concerning the afterlife, to which he replied only that the retribution for good and evil is like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound, and said nothing more.

The lady questioned him about this, but he never answered. Nevertheless, whenever an event was about to occur before it had even sprouted, he would always know of it in advance and would secretly make preparations for it;
yet he never spoke of it openly. Even his brothers and wife were not informed of these matters. This continued for five or six years.
He felt it was extremely laborious. Later, when he encountered the mourning for Lady Longcheng, he immediately recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Because of this, he was no longer required to serve as an official of the underworld. Consequently, he spoke with great emphasis that among all the sūtras, the power of its merit is supreme;

he then commanded his descendants to maintain the recitation of the scripture. When the Duke reached an age where he did not know his destined lifespan, he immediately feigned illness and retired to his estate. At that time, the Left Prime Minister Su...
Liangsi. The Right Minister Wei Daipai and the Great General Li Chongxuan were both close relatives by marriage to the Duke.

They once requested that the Duke enter government service, but the Duke firmly declined and did not go. At that time, cruel officials were in power and engaged in much false accusation and entrapment;
although the Duke had retired to his rural estate, because his marriage ties connected him to powerful nobles, he was subsequently slandered by a group of unruly elements.

He was informed [of his innocence]. Although the Master was repeatedly confined in prison, he felt no anxiety or distress; day and night he recited the scriptures, never ceasing his voice. Within a few days, he was indeed exonerated.
Others all followed his example, so it need not be recounted further. Both those within and without the court were struck with amazement and sighed in shared wonder.
When the Master reached the age of eighty-four and fell ill, approaching death, he still continued his recitation of the sutras without ceasing.
When his life was at its end, his spirit remained clear and lucid. Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, its pervasive and sweet aroma such as had never been heard of in this age.
The Master himself said that a transformed being (a *nirmāṇakāya*) had come to welcome him, and that he was to depart for the pure realm of the West.
Having thus bid farewell to his relatives, he passed away upon finishing his words. (This was personally recounted by his grandson, Yu Ni, the District Magistrate of Qi County in Zizhou.)
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, there was a man in the capital who died and revived after several days.
He recounted that before the infernal official, he had been subjected to interrogation and cross-examination. Suddenly, an officer sent to track down fugitives arrived;

the official rebuked him for failing to apprehend his quarry and was about to whip him when the tracking officer protested loudly, saying, "General Wei Xun upholds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
He recited [the scripture] constantly without ceasing. Good spirits protected him, surrounding him in several layers, making it impossible for anyone to seize him. Indeed, he was not lax.

The officials of the netherworld then sent someone to investigate and verify the matter, just as the words of the pursuers had stated; consequently, the pursuit was abandoned, and everyone praised him in unison.
Wei Xun was a native of Julu. His father, Shangde, was upright and frugal, devoted to learning without weariness, and particularly proficient in the Buddhist scriptures;
he also recited and upheld this sutra. In the Tianshou era, he passed away while serving as a Left Palace Attendant. His son, Xun, succeeded to his father’s legacy.

Upon shedding his plain white robes, he was appointed as a Military Aide (Canjun) of Bozhou. At that time, Wang of Langya rose in rebellion, and Liu Shou was appointed a false General of the Lang. He ordered—

He resisted the imperial army; moved by the intensity of his loyalty and filial piety, he turned from rebellion to submission. He lay hidden by day and traveled by night, avoiding the regular roads, and thus succeeded in reaching the capital.
On that day, he was summoned to an audience and granted the fifth rank, appointed as the *Simǎ* (Vice Governor) of Bō Prefecture, and immediately dispatched to suppress and pacify Bō Prefecture.

Summoned back to court, he was promoted to *Shàngyì Fèngyù* (Palace Attendant for Robes), serving both within and without the palace. Having successively held both civil and military posts, [this occurred] at the beginning of the Shénlóng era.
He was promoted by three ranks and appointed as Right General of the Gate Guard. Later, he was sent out as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Muzhou.
On account of official business, he was demoted to the rank of Vice Governor (Biejia) of Xuzhou. (Recorded by Zheng Shugou, Director of the Office of Personnel in Zizhou.)
Zhang Xuansu, the Magistrate of Huangmei County in Qi Prefecture, was twenty years old when he began to receive and uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Whenever his family encountered misfortune or illness, he would pray with a sincere heart; immediately, blessings and assistance would manifest in a most profound and efficacious manner.
All were healed and delivered. At over seventy years of age, he fell ill at Guocheng Village, some ten li east of Luocheng.
As his end approached, he beheld incense, flowers, banners, and canopies descending from the sky. With palms joined in joy, he immediately bathed and adorned himself;
the entire family likewise smelled a fragrant scent that did not cease for several days. (As told by Liu Jun, former Assistant Magistrate of Tongquan County in Zizhou.)
Xue Yan, the Sima of E (pronounced "e") Prefecture, upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with firm and pure faith.
When the time of his death arrived—he was over seventy years old—there appeared banners, canopies, flutes, and pipes that came through the air to welcome him. His wife witnessed this.
He followed after the banners and canopies. As his illness deepened and he grew increasingly frail, his wife called out to him from afar in the air.

He drifted upward as if riding upon clouds, ascending slowly and steadily into the distance. A continuous fragrance did not cease, which the entire family smelled together; he subsequently passed away.
This, too, was an inconceivable event (as previously related by Liu Jun).

Yao Dai, a native of Qi County in Zizhou, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra*. In the fourth year of the Chang’an era (728 CE), while observing the period of mourning for his deceased father, he made a vow to personally transcribe the four great divisions of the Buddhist canon (*catvāri mahā-vaipulya-sūtrāṇi*)—one copy each of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*—for the sake of his late father.
He had finished transcribing ten fascicles of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* and one hundred fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

While he was transcribing the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, having completed fourteen fascicles, at the hour of midday, a deer suddenly burst through the door and entered. It stood before the sutra-stand, raised its head, and licked the desk.
Having finished licking the desk, it immediately crouched beneath the stand. There were five or six dogs in the house; seeing the deer, they wagged their tails but did not [attack it].
He dared not bark. When Yao waited for him to descend from the bed, he picked him up and he was not startled or afraid. [Yao] conferred the Three Refuges upon him;
he leaped about and curled his paws, and though released, he would not leave. By the Tianxian era, when all the scriptures were completed, he wrapped them all in his fur.
Just as he was about to place them into the case, a butcher named Li Huinu appeared for no apparent reason and suddenly arrived, standing at the table.
He stepped forward, pointed at the sutra, and laughed; he stood with palms joined, desiring to take the scripture. That butcher’s mouth was foul and his ears were deaf;
both eyes were bloodshot, and he was addicted to wine and violent by nature—few are his like.

The sutras he had transcribed all had their rollers adorned with lapis lazuli, but the Prajñāpāramitā Sutra alone was decorated with plain sandalwood. He simply selected the plain roller, thereby revealing that this man [was devoted] to the Prajñā[pāramitā].
If there was an opportunity, he would wait until [the butcher] had finished wrapping it in white paper and placing it in a lacquered box;
then, the butcher would hold his knife across the top of the scripture box and drive off laughing. Once he had gone, he was never seen again, and no one knew where he had gone.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong visited the Daoist Zhu Fayin, who was exceptionally learned in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, at Meezhou.
After lecturing for many years, he finally returned home. At that time, more than twenty local scholars came to pay their respects and inquire after him.
His friend Wang Chao, a district magistrate, had ordered his servant to slaughter a whole carcass of sheep; the meat was placed in a bag and cooked until it was done.
In his heart he knew they were going to kill him, yet he could not bear his hunger and ate accordingly. He consumed no more than four or five pieces of meat.
After a day had passed, at the time of mid-afternoon (dié), his belly suddenly grew hot and his head began to ache; his limbs felt as if they were being cut away.
By the time of dusk, his condition became increasingly grave and debilitating. Outside the door, he heard the sound of someone calling out, "Wait for Yao!"
Although his heart did not wish to go out and look, he was unaware that his body had already gone outside.

When asked what business he had, a messenger in yellow robes—whose appearance was like that of a provincial governor (cishi) wielding a sword—called out to him and then departed immediately. As he waited outside the gate, there was a stream;
at the moment of his departure, however, neither the stream nor the ravine was seen, but only a level, broad road with rows of trees on both sides, which he traveled for three or four [li].
Li saw a great city, which was said to be the city of Zizhou. Its city walls featured double walkways and multi-storied pavilions, with white plastered walls and vermilion pillars;
it was also exceedingly beautiful. He further questioned the messenger, who replied, "This is not the city of Zizhou," and instructed him not to speak.
The city had five successive gates, each flanked on both sides by gatehouses, with the gates facing one another. Above each gate, there were inscriptions.

The inscription on the lintel resembles seal script (*zhuànshū*), yet its characters cannot be deciphered. Although the gates are numerous, not a single guard is present; the streets and alleys are likewise deserted.
The messenger enters within five layers of gates and finds a great hall. The corridors and buildings are lofty and imposing; both the hall and its doors are unguarded.
Upon reaching the outer edge of a screen wall, he peers inside and sees a person in purple robes upon the dais. His body—

He was somewhat stout and his countenance was handsome and elegant, appearing as if he were under thirty. When the messenger entered and announced, "Yao Dai has arrived," Dai rushed in and prostrated from a distance.
With glaring eyes and a harsh voice, [the deity] asked, "For what reason have you summoned so many people? You kill them in a pure place and eat them!
Dai pondered this but could not understand the matter; he saw only his wrathful anger, with fire emanating from both his eyes and his mouth.
Guang was terrified and panicked, not knowing how to respond. He immediately explained, "Lately, I have only been reciting sutras;
I have neither killed anyone nor eaten human flesh. The other then asked, "Which sutra do you recite? He replied, "I recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
The person wearing purple, hearing Yao wait for this explanation, smiled with joy and said, "Excellent! As he spoke, someone suddenly appeared beside him wearing yellow;
though his hands and feet were not visible, he held an object about two chi in length, composed of eight layers.
It was like striking a drum with a mallet; he cried out in a loud voice, "How could you eat meat in Master Zhu’s room? He did not dare conceal it and admitted that he had indeed eaten it.
When asked how much he had eaten, he replied, "I ate five or six pieces. The man dressed in purple turned his gaze back toward the man in yellow robes.

The man replied, "He ate four taels and eight zhu. He then took up his brush and wrote [the words] into the man's ear; from afar, the sound was heard. [The official thought,] "This matter is not as I intended.

Let him go for now, and wait until the day Cao arrives at the Prefectural Office to interrogate him. The man dressed in purple spoke again, saying, "The Buddha hall of Dayun Temple has been commissioned for early repair and shall be completed.
He responded with an assent and ran out, having gone only five or six paces when he saw one [person] at the western end of the hall.
A man was bound in shackles and fetters, with four nails driven into his armor-plates. He asked for Yao Dai (Yao Daishi).
A person in the hall called out, "Yao Gongcao, come back!"—not calling him by the name Dai. Looking at the one wearing the shackles, it was none other than the butcher Li Huinuo.
A person dressed in purple asked, "Is it true or false that this man has read the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? He replied, "It is true. Having finished answering, he looked back and saw only emptiness.
The cangue lay upon the ground, yet no butcher was to be seen. When he first entered, there was no one guarding the hall or the gate;
yet by the time he emerged, there were several thousand people on both sides of the hall, dressed in crimson, purple, yellow, and green, each standing in their respective ranks.
There were also many women, some carrying cangues and others bearing chains; some were bound hand and foot, while others had their heads confined in cages. Thus it was.
In the midst of the assembly, he saw his relative, Zhang Kai, also present among them. Although he was wearing a small cangue, it lacked nails or metal plates.

He prostrated himself, requesting that scriptures be prepared for him at home and asking that he not speak much. As he wished to move forward, he was restrained by others and not permitted to proceed.
Among them was one man with his waistband loosened and head bare who said to the attendant, "Go quickly; this is no place for conversation."
As he was returning, he saw that the man was actually Zhang Xian, a villager from the neighboring village of Dazhuang.
He had been ill for many years and could not take even water or gruel into his mouth; those of the local community who saw him all spoke of his certain death.

His wife, children, and relatives had already prepared the funeral implements. After Yao Da woke up, he told his son to transcribe a scripture for him. Less than ten days later, his illness was cured.
"Let her go! Let her out beyond the inner wall! At every gate, men stood in solemn ranks, brandishing swords, spears, bows, and arrows, ready to seize her;
they would not let her pass until she had reached her biological father, who came running from the east side of the hall, crying out:
"My son has been released without incident. Why did you obstruct him and not let him go? Let him wait until he can stretch out his arm so that I may show it to him.
He immediately rolled up his sleeves and extended his arm for him to see; thus, he was able to leave. When he woke up, a full day had already passed.
There was one named Yang Jian, a native of Tongquan County in Zizhou. He possessed a profound understanding of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and constantly lectured upon it throughout Shu.

Furthermore, he regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Once, while traveling on foot with birds flying overhead as the sun was already setting and the road was infested with fierce beasts, everyone else was filled with dread.
Jian, however, continued to recite the sūtra aloud while walking at a swift pace. He encountered a man who could see ghosts, who marveled at him...
The ghosts fled in a panic as if terrified of something, until they encountered Yang Jian, who was walking along reciting the sutra. The ghosts were struck with alarm;
by the power of the sutra, it was known that wherever it is recited, it is protected and sustained by all the Buddhas.
Li Qiuyi, Assistant Magistrate of Gaoyou County in Yangzhou, died on the twenty-ninth day of the second month in the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era.
He passed away suddenly after contracting a severe illness. At the moment of his death, two men came to summon him, saying, "We are surnamed Duan;

we do not state our given names, but we simply say we are here to summon you by royal command. You are not permitted to stay even for a moment. At that time, there were five others who were also being summoned.
There were over a hundred people; the men all wore wooden neck-fetters (*kāṣa*), and the women were all bound with their hands behind their backs. They were driven forward together for several *li*.

There was a man riding a white horse and wearing crimson robes, holding a bow and arrows in his hand, who cried out in a loud voice: "Qiūyī, you are difficult to pursue! Why did you not put on your fetters? Qiūyī immediately consulted with the Commissioner Duàn.
[He explained that] his grandfather held a fifth-grade rank and he himself was currently serving as an official, so it was not appropriate [for him to wear them].
As he was still speaking, his entire body was suddenly bound with chains, and he knew not why.
After traveling another ten-odd *li*, he saw several dozen large locust trees, beneath each of which stood a horse trough. He immediately asked the official Duan, "What place is this?
Duan replied, "The Great Deity of the Five Paths records the conditions of the human realm; we halt our horses here. Qiu—
Upon hearing this, he finally realized he was dead. Encouraged to proceed, he eventually arrived at the king’s gate, where he saw a man holding a legal document, his countenance filled with urgency.
The man said to the messenger Duan, "The King has sent me to pursue you; why have you been so late?
The messenger Duan did not dare speak further, and immediately took Qiu Yifeng and the chief clerk of the case. He addressed Qiu Yiyu, saying, "This man's surname is Jiao and his name is Ce."
"This gentleman is the presiding official of this case; you may go with him to see the King. Jiao Ce immediately led him to the audience.
When the King saw Qiu Yi arrive, he rebuked him angrily, saying, "Li Shiyan has gathered his kinsmen and slaughtered the lives of others for his own amusement, showing no sense of shame or remorse.
The name "Shiyan" was actually Qiu’s minor given name. Shortly thereafter, the animals that had been killed appeared before him.
They all spoke in human voices. "We, such-and-such individuals, have now come to avenge our enemies.
Great King, how shall you dispose of this? Jiaodu immediately stepped forward and consulted the King. Li Shi said, "It is not yet fitting for them to die.

Because those who were killed desire to be quickly assigned to their place of rebirth, they have come to face judgment. The King asked himself, "Throughout your entire life, what meritorious deeds have you performed? Recite [them]."
Whether or not one upholds this most supreme and foremost sutra: I recall that during my previous life, I performed no meritorious deeds, doing nothing but releasing hawks and dogs.
Suddenly, I remembered having commissioned a single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the past.

Upon hearing the name of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the King immediately rose, joined his palms, and called Yì to ascend the steps. In the darkness, he invoked the name of the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the "most supreme and foremost merit."
He spoke to the beast from the *Dejing* (Scripture on Virtue), saying, "Stay back for now; summon Jiao Ce and lead him to the repository of scriptures to examine them.
Beside the king's hall was a place that appeared to have no boundaries, in the center of which stood a palace adorned with the seven treasures.
He ordered Qiu to ascend the palace and draw a single scroll of scripture from within the collection to open and read; it was indeed Qiu.
In addition to the single copy of a scripture he had written, another document was discovered: a petition for inviting monks. This was the place where Qiu Yi had performed his writing.
When asked by Jiao Du, he replied, "Throughout my life, I have also performed various meritorious deeds several times. For what reason do I see only these two places?
As an official, I took money through illegal means and oppressed the poor and weak; these were impure things. The merit I cultivated from such sources is naturally exhausted."

The Master did not oppose the official business and returned with them to see the King. The King asked whether the sutras he had transcribed were authentic and said, "You may summon the slaughtered animals here.
The Master declined politely, saying only that he was permitted to have the sutras made for him and that the animals would ultimately not remain there.

After a short while, the slaughtered animals all arrived together before the King. The King sent a monk to commission the making of Prajñāpāramitā sutras on their behalf; thus it was with those animals.
They were born together and then dispersed. The King said, "This merit is inexhaustible. Tell Jiao Ce that he may be released immediately;
do not detain him further. He sent him out beyond the city gate. Repeatedly grasping Qiu Yi’s hand, Jiao Ce exerted all his strength until he could finally let go.
Qiu Yi promised to give Ce three hundred strings of cash, which was all he had in his home at that time. It was indeed true.
"I dare not begrudge it. To repay Master Qiu for his single word of advice, even if you were to ask for ten thousand strings of cash, it would ultimately be of no benefit.

I beg you, sir, to commission twenty copies of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for my sake. Qiu immediately granted his permission. He further said, "Although I am a minister of the underworld, I have endured extreme hardship.
Without the aid of merit, it will be difficult for me to take rebirth. You must strive to transcribe these scriptures for me; I hope you will not fail to do so."
Zhi Ce urged him along the path, and they proceeded further. Ce pointed out a spot; looking down, it was deep and pitch black.
Zhi refused to enter, but Ce pushed him into the dark pit. Startled and terrified, his eyes opened, and he found himself inside a coffin.
Exhausted, he could not speak for a long time. Hearing the sounds of men and women weeping, he whispered softly to report: "Do not weep; I am now alive."

Qiu Yi’s younger sister-in-law, Du Yin, served as a military aide (*canjunshi*) in Nanzhou. Knowing that the funeral encoffining was scheduled for the fourth day of the third month, she came to observe the proceedings.
Although she heard voices, she did not permit the coffin to be opened for inspection, stating, "This is a reanimated corpse; you must not approach it.
Her sons and daughters, however, disregarded their uncle’s words and proceeded to open the coffin. Qiu Yi narrowly escaped with his life.
He moved his body out of the coffin and recounted the events of the underworld in detail for three days.
On the eighth day of the third month, all members of the family, both young and old, donated their clothing and all their funds to invite monks to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
They commissioned one hundred scrolls for the sake of all their enemies and twenty scrolls for Jiao Du; however, before these were finished, one night someone struck him.
He went to the gate and announced, "This is Jiao Ce. Qiu Yi immediately ordered that he be told: "I am currently in the midst of copying [the scriptures] and shall soon finish.
I will certainly not let you down; why must you come again? Ce replied, "Please report to Minister Li: there is nothing else. I have been honored by you for creating scriptures on my behalf."

Having already entrusted his soul to rebirth, he came to bid farewell. Xue Huaiyuan, the high official of Yangzhou, knowing that Qiu had returned to life twice, summoned him to inquire about matters of the underworld.
He recorded everything in detail and presented it for the Emperor’s hearing. By imperial decree, Qiu was granted an increase in rank and bestowed with the fifth grade.
He was dispatched by express courier from Jiazhou to Daozhao Commandery; while passing through Zizhou, as the weather was hot, he went to Yao Daitingzi to seek coolness. [The Emperor] personally...
To be discussed later. Furthermore, he left behind a handwritten copy. The eulogy says: "Ah!
The Great Sage—his wondrous wisdom is identical [to ours]. Responding without a mind, he penetrates without a thought.
He does not exhaust himself in existence, nor does he dwell in emptiness. Without deliberation or anxiety, he achieves all success."
Chapter Six: On Sincerity (with preface, ten sections).

In the past, Duke Jing of Song shifted the stars, and Lü Yang turned back the sun. Meng Zong caused bamboo shoots to sprout during the season of ice, and Liu Yin gathered *jin* mushrooms amidst the frost.
When Wang Liang spoke of clouds, they gathered even before his words had ended; when the rain for Jiangshan fell, it followed the path of his carriage.

Reaching them all, they are universally moistened. How much more so for those who are without reception and without mind! Sincerity ensures a certain response; non-action and non-attainment lead to a spontaneous penetration.

Practicing compassion that is free from attachment, profound benevolence is universally harmonized. Guiding with wisdom that is beyond knowing, the sages and worthies oversee this far-reaching influence.

There is no virtue that does not encompass even the most distant realms—how could it be limited to the three worlds? There is no clarity that does not perceive even the most obscure places—how could it stop at the ten directions?
Therefore, the chapter "Responding with Sincerity" is appended hereafter.
The monk Qingxu of Huiyi Monastery in Zizhou, whose secular surname was Tang, [composed this] during the sixth month of the first year of the Shengli era.
While he was in Yuzhou, a severe drought occurred. Officials and commoners alike prayed for rain without success; the people were filled with anxiety, not knowing where to turn.
The monk then entered the meditation hall before the Buddha and made a sincere invocation, praying that the great compassion of all Buddhas might be bestowed upon them.
The Dragon King was filled with joy and sent down sweet rain to rescue and relieve all living beings.

When the disciple reached noon on the following day, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* one hundred times for the sake of the Dragon Kings and others, vowing that sweet rain would fall early at noon.

When the time of noon arrived and his recitation of the sutra was finished, the heavens immediately sent down rain; the ditches and canals overflowed, and the plains and marshes were everywhere flooded.
The moisture was abundant and pervasive; its efficacy was such as this.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Shengli era, Qingxu was staying at Changle Mountain in Tongbai County, Tangzhou, observing the summer retreat at Changle Temple.
It happened that there was a drought, and the five grains were withered and curled. The local people beat drums and set fires upon the mountains for this reason.
He prayed for rain. He sought it for ten days, yet there was no sign or response whatsoever. Consequently, he took muddy water into the monastery, intending to sprinkle it upon the monks.
One of the monks informed him, saying, "Donor, do not defile the venerable masters. It is I, a poor monk, who have been praying for rain on behalf of you, the donor."
"It will surely be sufficient by tomorrow. From the noon of the twentieth day of the fifth month, he entered the ritual hall to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
By the time of midday the following day, rain had begun to fall; in a mere moment, it was sufficient for all, moistening both high and low lands everywhere.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Dazhu era, a period of extreme drought occurred.
By imperial decree, the prefectures and counties were ordered to pray for rain, and twenty monks from the capital were assembled to offer supplications; yet not a single drop fell.

Among them was the monk Qingxu, who went to Fengguo Temple to see Master Fuli and discuss the matter of praying for rain. Fuli then asked the monk, "Master, what method do you employ to pray for rain?"
The monk replied, "Recite the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Dharani and the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra with a focused mind;
by this, pray for rain. [The official] asked, "In how many days will there be sufficient rain? He answered, "In three days and three nights, the rain will surely be sufficient.
[The official] prostrated again and said resentfully, "Even if you pray for seven days, if it does not rain within those seven days, I shall send you away."
He had Xue Jichang placed in shackles around his neck and said, "I shall send you off as a starving ghost. Upon hearing these words, the monk’s resolve was further strengthened.
He informed Bao Fu-li, saying, "At the time of the morning meal tomorrow, the rain will not yet have ceased; before three full days have passed, the rain will surely fall everywhere."

The monk immediately entered the ritual arena and recited the mantra with a sincere heart. By the time the next day’s mealtime arrived, rain began to fall, reaching a depth of four or five inches, after which it cleared once again.
He then paid his respects to his disciple Yuanjì and said to Qingxū, "Tomorrow marks the completion of the three-day period.
Now I see that there are no clouds for ten li; I do not know what signs you, Master, will use as proof."
He replied, "Do not worry; within three days the rain will surely be sufficient. When the following day arrived toward evening, there was still not a single cloud in the sky.

His mind became pure and earnest, and fearing that no efficacy would be manifested, he again addressed the great Bodhisattvas, Arhats, Holy Sangha, and all worthy sages and disciples of the ten directions:
"Today, with a single mind, for the sake of the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm..."
He prayed for rain. He vowed, "If the rain tonight is insufficient, I shall give up my life here for the sake of all living beings.
Thereupon, with utmost sincerity and devotion, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. When the second watch was nearly over, the rain began to pour down in torrents.
By dawn, it had reached more than a foot in depth throughout a circumference of five hundred li; the sweet moisture was sufficient everywhere. This was the power of his majestic spiritual efficacy.
It was as majestic as this. From that point on, he prayed for rain and subsequently spent the summer retreat at Fengguo Temple.
During the second and third months of winter that year, there was neither snow nor rain. Vinaya Master Huishen again sent a request for snow;
with single-minded devotion, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. After three days, he was once more blessed by Heaven with a fall of snow. Such was his spiritual efficacy.
It was thus: in the third year of the Chang’an era, Qingxu sat out the summer retreat at Wuzhen Temple.
When it reached the twentieth day of the seventh month, he briefly entered the city and stayed at Ziseng Temple. On the first day of the eighth month, a great rain fell, continuing until the fifth.
The sun did not shine; rice and wheat surged in price; carts and oxen could not pass; the common people were driven to desperation, knowing no means of livelihood.
That monk, until the fifth watch of the night, forgot both sleep and food. At dawn, he solemnly took up his incense burner and entered the Buddha hall.
Just as he was about to offer a petition and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* to stop the rain, three or five monks came down from the hall and saw him, saying to him:
The monk asked, "Master, what do you intend to do? [The other] replied, "I wish to recite mantras to stop the rain.
The monks all said, "You might be able to stop it yourself, but why make such a fuss? The monk answered, "This is also a matter difficult to believe.
Let us bet two strings of cash against one string; let us double our wager with this master. We shall set a time limit for each, so there is no need to wait until it grows dark. Thus spoke the monk.

The word "etcetera" (et cetera) implies that you may stop once it has become dark; I shall grant you one *guan* as a reward. Qingxu replied, "If I recite ten times, the rain will cease for the time being.
If I recite fifteen times, I shall cause the clouds to rise high. At twenty recitations, I shall cause the sun to emerge.
At twenty-five recitations, the clouds on all four sides will disperse. At thirty recitations, the clouds will be entirely cleared away. The monk [then began].
Upon hearing these words, [the man] immediately took up the monk’s robe and departed.
Having uttered such a deceitful statement, he did not even realize that his own previous life had been burdened with many offenses against the Sangha, which caused him to speak these words.
The monk then entered the ritual arena and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. When he reached the tenth recitation, the rain ceased. By the fifteenth recitation, the clouds...
The sun rose high. When it reached the twentieth repetition, the monks saw this slight anomaly and were all struck with alarm.
At the twenty-fifth repetition, the clouds on all four sides dispersed at once; the assembly of monks cried out in unison, losing their voices.
By the thirtieth repetition, the clouds had vanished entirely. The monks rose up all at once, intending to bind the monk, but he replied, "You are not [the ones who can]."

Sāgara Dragon King: "Whether it is clear weather or rain depends on you; whether it is thunder or rain depends on you. Among them was one who understood the matter, and after he rebuked him with anger, [the other] finally desisted.
Alas! The majestic power of Prajñā cannot be fully described in words. When those of inferior capacity hear the Way, they will surely laugh at it in derision.
In the third year of [the reign of] Chang’an, during the tenth month, the Imperial carriage traveled to [blank]. By the end of the eleventh month, Qingxu was staying at Zhongxiang Temple.
From the tenth month until the [blank] month, there had been no snow. The monastic community of Zhongxiang Temple requested that Qingxu pray for snow.
The monk immediately entered the ritual hall and, with single-minded devotion, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, setting a limit of three days.
He prayed for snow within [the monastery], and after reciting [the mantra] for three full days, Heaven sent down a heavy snowfall for one day and one night. Both near and far, all were satisfied.
This, too, was a miraculous manifestation of the Prajñāpāramitā.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year of the Chang’an era, Master Benping submitted a memorial concerning Qingxu.

Because the Great Saint Empress Dowager was suffering from a wind ailment, Qingxu entered the palace for twenty-one days of recitation and chanting. The Emperor issued an imperial inquiry: "Master, are you a resident monk of this monastery, or a visiting monk?"
He then replied, "I am a monk residing at this temple. The princess and her attendants said to the monk, "Master, you have deceived the Imperial Decree;
you are truly guilty of a great offense. For now, let the Master go. The monk felt deep regret, lamenting his own meager merit for having mistakenly addressed a holy personage.
He immediately entered the meditation hall and requested a single object of focus, vowing to recite only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for one day and one night.
During the night, he dreamed of two monks heading toward the Chan courtyard of the Zhongxiang Monastery.

They asked the master of the house, "We do not know whether the master named Qingxu has established himself yet, nor whether his name has been registered in the monastic records of the Ministry of Sacrifices. The master replied, "It seems it has not yet been done. The monks—
He said to Qingxu: "I shall bestow a name upon you, Master, when the sun sets. Then, during the tenth month of the third year of the Shenglong era, the Imperial carriage visited Chang'an;
yet in the twelfth month, there was neither snow nor rain. At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master from Qizhou and the Ācārya Yang Jun were present.

He petitioned that the monk be permitted to enter the palace to recite sutras for two seven-day periods. Emperor Ying Tianxing immediately dispatched Qingxu, allowing him to choose a temple to reside in.
As for the mention of "the sun setting," it was intended to signify the Emperor’s own return to the West. Through the spiritual power of Prajñā, there is no wish that shall not be fulfilled.
In the first year of the Shénlóng era, Zuo Bùquè Zhào Yánxǐ submitted a memorial stating that Qīngxū had entered the palace to pray for rain.
After he had been inside for three nights, he was deceived by a *gòngfèng* monk who led him to the palace hall of City, to a place suitable for establishing a *dàochǎng*.
The monk did not understand this and immediately proceeded forward. The six monks let the Master out to the exterior;
he prayed and emerged, heading toward Mount Nan within the Wangchun Palace. There was a Maitreya Pavilion there, and he prayed for rain at that location.

As soon as he entered the ritual hall, the clouds gathered and then dispersed. Within three days, he felt utterly exhausted and went down to the bottom of a mountain stream to take water and wash himself.
[His] face was turned [downward]. Because he was lying down, his eyes were closed. He saw a temple attendant holding a staff and striking the monk’s head.

"Master, why are you here? Why are you lying on the ground? The monk exerted himself and forced himself up; he immediately rose and returned to the lower hall, reciting the scriptures with all his heart.
When the sun reached the west, clouds gathered from all four directions. Not more than a moment passed before a great rain suddenly fell. Directly...
By the time morning arrived, the rain had fallen sufficiently everywhere.
Lü Wenzhan, the Assistant Magistrate of Langzhong County in Langzhou, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* more than thirty thousand times;

his spiritual efficacy was like that of a deity. Six or seven years ago, one of his teeth fell out for no apparent reason. He made a vow with utmost sincerity, and the tooth immediately began to grow back gradually.
It grew gradually; by now it has reached about half its full length. On the second day of the first month in the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, the sprout again fell off without cause.
He made his vow as before, and the sprout subsequently grew back. That a sprout should grow on what is old is surely due to divine assistance.
In the third year of the Kaiyuan era, during the height of summer, there was a severe drought; the grasses and trees were withered and yellow.
The Regional Inspector Liu Yuan ordered him to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with a focused mind. Before it was finished, a copious rain fell, moistening everything;

far and near, all were satisfied, and the harvests for that year were bountiful. In the spring of that same year, heavy rain damaged the silkworms and wheat. The Vice-Governor Wei Ezizi also ordered [him to recite].
Wen then unfurled the scripture and recited it; immediately, the weather became clear and bright.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the region suffered from a severe drought, and the Regional Inspector Liu Xiaozhong was sent down to order another prayer for rain.
From the hour of the horse (noon) until the hour of the monkey (7 p.m.), a fine drizzle fell lightly. By the time of the first watch of the night, the sky became clear and bright.

Thereupon, in the courtyard before him, he made a vow with a sincere heart and recited the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; before he had finished a single fascicle, the rain fell everywhere, saturating both the high and the low ground.
On the twentieth day of the first month in the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, the weather was overcast with rain.

The Prefect Liu Yuan, considering that the following day was a Jiazi day and fearing that if it continued to rain the monasteries might suffer from drought, ordered Wen-zhan to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and pray with a sincere heart for clear skies. He opened the scriptures, and immediately the rain cleared. On the Jiazi day, the heavens...
It was exceedingly clear. Such is the power of Prajñā; its response is as swift as a flash. The eulogy says:
The Way has one essence, yet its manifestations appear as the three bodies. Its transformation extends ever further, and its virtue becomes ever more true.
By forgetting the mind one attains sagehood; by non-thought one becomes divine. Through sincerity alone and through earnestness, the response is reached.

(Colophon states: On the lower part of the seventh month in the first year of the Chōkwan era, the śramaṇa Shōkan transcribed this.
Completed the first proofreading on the seventh day of the eighth month of the same year.
